question: Why does ChannelDelivery use a single status enum (pending/sent/dead_letter/canceled) instead of a separate transient 'failed' status next to a boolean 'willRetry' flag?
answer_hinglish:
Decision PLAN.md mein clearly likha hai: ek status enum, do field nahi. Agar ek alag 'failed' status hota ek 'willRetry' boolean ke saath, toh woh sirf 'pending' kehne ka doosra, zyada complicated tarika hota -- ek failed attempt jiske paas retries bache hain, woh conceptually EXACTLY wahi state mein hai jaisa woh apne pehle attempt se pehle tha: woh apne next attempt ka wait kar raha hai. Isliye is repo ka rule hai 'a status field with guarded transitions is enough' (projects 21/22 mein bhi yehi pattern hai).

Agar do fields hote (status='failed' + willRetry=true/false), tab ek naya risk aata: dono fields ko hamesha SYNC rakhna padta -- ek jagah status update ho jaaye aur willRetry update hona bhool jaaye, toh ek inconsistent state ban jaata jisko catch karna mushtkil hota. Single enum mein yeh risk hi exist nahi karta kyunki sirf EK field hai jo transition karta hai.

Actual implementation src/scheduler.ts ke dispatchChannel mein hai: jab provider.send() fail hota hai, delivery.lastError set hota hai, aur phir sirf ek check hota hai -- `attempts >= maxAttempts` toh 'dead_letter', nahi toh status 'pending' hi rehta hai (sirf nextAttemptAt update hota hai backoff ke saath). Koi intermediate 'failed' state kabhi bani hi nahi -- dispatch ke beech mein bhi status 'pending' hi dikhta hai.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate samajhta hai redundant state fields ka risk, aur 'single source of truth' principle kaise status design mein apply hota hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek delivery package ka status 'in transit' hi rehta hai jab tak woh 'delivered' ya 'returned to sender' na ho jaaye -- beech mein ek baar truck breakdown hua ya nahi, yeh ek alag 'breakdown-happened' flag nahi banata, package abhi bhi 'in transit' hi hai.
how_it_works: ChannelStatus = pending | sent | dead_letter | canceled. attempts aur nextAttemptAt diagnostic/scheduling info carry karte hain bina status ko change kiye jab tak koi terminal transition (sent ya dead_letter) na ho.
in_this_project: src/types.ts ka ChannelStatus type aur src/scheduler.ts ka dispatchChannel -- failure path mein status sirf dead_letter ya pending set hota hai, koi third transient value nahi.
code_example:
// real, src/types.ts
export type ChannelStatus = "pending" | "sent" | "dead_letter" | "canceled";
advantages: Ek hi field, koi sync risk do fields ke beech
Guarded transitions se invalid states (jaise sent+willRetry=true) possible hi nahi
Simpler tests -- sirf ek field assert karna padta hai
disadvantages: Caller ko 'is this pending because it never started, or because a retry is coming' jaanne ke liye attempts field bhi dekhna padta hai
Ek naya consumer status ko standalone dekh kar confuse ho sakta hai agar woh attempts/nextAttemptAt na dekhe
common_mistakes: Do fields banana jo ek doosre se out of sync ho sakte hain
Yeh sochna ki 'failed' ek terminal state hai -- yahan sirf dead_letter terminal hai
Status ko dispatch ke BEECH mein temporarily 'failed' set karna, jo race conditions ke liye extra surface banata
follow_up_questions: If you needed to distinguish 'never attempted' from 'failed, awaiting retry' in the API response, how would you do it without adding a new status value?
What would a State pattern implementation of ChannelDelivery look like here, and why did this project avoid it?

question: Why is due-post dispatch a polled tick() instead of a job queue with leases, like project 21's stage 2?
answer_hinglish:
PLAN.md mein yeh explicitly compare kiya gaya hai project 21 (notification) stage 2 ke saath. Lease-based job queue ka poora point yeh hai ki MULTIPLE WORKERS ek SHARED queue se job 'claim' kar sakein, aur agar ek worker crash/stall ho jaaye, uska claimed job timeout ke baad DOOSRE worker ko mil jaaye. Yeh problem is project ke stage 1 mein exist hi nahi karti -- sirf EK caller hai jo tick() drive karta hai, kabhi doosra worker uska job 'steal' nahi karega.

Jo problem yahan actually exist karti hai: SAME caller ka tick() dobara call ho jaana jabki pehla abhi ek slow provider ka wait kar raha hai (ya ek cancel usi waqt race kare). Iske liye poora lease/claim-token system overkill hai -- ek lightweight 'dispatching' Set (sirf "postId:channel" keys currently in-flight) kaafi hai, bahut kam complexity ke saath.

tick() khud simple hai: due channels scan karo, unko dispatching set mein add karo, Promise.all se saari dispatchChannel() calls chalao, finally mein set se remove karo. Agar kabhi multiple WORKER PROCESSES same scheduler ko drive karna pade (stage 2, if it happens), PLAN.md khud kehta hai ki project 21 ka lease/claim-token design reused hoga wholesale, redesign nahi.
why_needed: Interviewer samajhna chahta hai ki candidate 'YAGNI' (you aren't gonna need it) ko architecture decision ke roop mein apply kar sakta hai -- sahi complexity level choose karna, requirement ke hisaab se.
real_world_analogy: Ek chhoti dukaan mein ek hi salesperson hai jo order list dekh kar kaam karta hai -- usse kisi 'token system' ki zaroorat nahi jo bataye kaunsa order kiska hai, kyunki koi doosra salesperson hai hi nahi jo wahi order utha le.
how_it_works: tick() poll karta hai due+pending channels, dispatching Set same-caller overlap se bachata hai. Koi lease timeout, koi claim token, koi 'another worker stole this' scenario nahi hai.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka tick() method aur dispatching Set -- compare project 21 ke src/queue.ts ka InMemoryJobQueue (claim/owns/complete/reschedule with leaseToken/leaseUntil).
advantages: Bahut kam complexity jab sirf ek caller hai
Testing easy hai -- koi lease timing simulate karne ki zaroorat nahi
Code directly readable hai, koi claim-token bookkeeping nahi
disadvantages: Multiple worker processes support nahi karta -- sab ek hi process mein tick() call karte hain
Agar scale badhe, poora redesign chahiye hoga (project 21 jaisa lease system laana padega)
common_mistakes: Chhoti scale ke liye bhi lease-based queue bana dena, jab zaroorat na ho
Yeh sochna ki dispatching Set multi-worker race ko bhi cover karta hai -- yeh sirf SAME caller ke overlap ke against hai
follow_up_questions: If a second process also started calling tick() on a separate in-memory instance, what would break?
What is the minimal change needed to make dispatchChannel work with project 21's lease-based queue instead of the dispatching Set?

question: Why is a channel just a string key into a providers map, instead of a closed enum of named platforms (linkedin, twitter, mastodon)?
answer_hinglish:
README mein pehla hi rule yeh hai: 'A channel is a string key into the providers map given to the constructor.' Agar ek closed enum hota (jaise `type Channel = "linkedin" | "twitter" | "mastodon"`), toh scheduler ko hardcoded pata hona padta kaunse platforms exist karte hain -- naya channel add karne ke liye scheduler ke TYPE ko hi change karna padta.

String-key design mein scheduler ko bilkul pata nahi hota channel ASLI mein kya hai -- usse sirf yeh pata hota hai ki `providers` object mein koi key registered hai usse handle karne ke liye. Yeh exactly Strategy pattern hai: FakeChannelProvider interface hi matter karta hai, implementation (AlwaysSucceeds/AlwaysFails/Flaky, ya kal koi real LinkedIn provider) scheduler ke liye invisible hai.

Validation iska downside cover karta hai: `schedulePost` ek unknown channel key ko `UNKNOWN_CHANNEL` error se reject karta hai, AT REQUEST TIME (construction ke baad kabhi bhi, jab tak provider registered nahi hai) -- isliye type-safety ka fayda (compile-time typo-catch) na hone ka trade-off ek clean runtime check se cover hota hai, dispatch time tak wait nahi karna padta.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate Strategy pattern aur runtime-vs-compile-time validation ka trade-off samajhta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek universal power socket adapter jo kisi bhi plug shape ko accept karta hai jab tak uske liye koi adapter attachment maujood ho -- socket khud nahi jaanta duniya mein kitne plug types hain, sirf yeh jaanta hai ki kaunsa adapter is waqt attached hai.
how_it_works: providers: Record<string, FakeChannelProvider> constructor mein diya jaata hai. requireValidChannels shape check ke baad har channel string ke liye this.providers[channel] exist karta hai ya nahi dekhta hai.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka SchedulerOptions.providers field aur requireValidChannels method; src/providers.ts ka FakeChannelProvider interface.
advantages: Naya channel add karna sirf providers map mein ek entry add karna hai, scheduler code change nahi hota
Strategy pattern -- scheduler kabhi provider ki real identity nahi jaanta
Request-time validation, dispatch time tak surprise nahi
disadvantages: Compile-time typo-catch nahi milta (jaise `"linkedn"` typo sirf runtime par UNKNOWN_CHANNEL dega)
IDE autocomplete nahi milta valid channel names ke liye
common_mistakes: Yeh sochna ki channel keys kahin globally defined hain -- woh sirf jo construction ke waqt providers mein diye gaye hain
Validation dispatch time tak defer karna instead of request time
follow_up_questions: What would a closed enum design cost you when adding a new platform later?
How does this design differ from a Strategy pattern used elsewhere in this repo, like FakeChannelProvider vs a real sender?

question: cancelChannel/cancelPost use a plain 'still pending' rule, but editPost requires zero attempts on every non-canceled channel. Why is editing stricter than canceling?
answer_hinglish:
PLAN.md mein yeh literally is paragraph mein diya gaya hai: dono rules 'only while still pending' ke READING hain, par edit ki reading strict hai. Cancel ke liye kuch 'undo' karne ki zaroorat NAHI hai -- ek provider call jo abhi tak hui hi nahi hai, usko future mein hone se rokna hai. Chahe channel mid-retry ho (attempts > 0, status pending), cancel safe hai kyunki ab koi aur attempt hoga hi nahi.

Edit alag hai kyunki CONTENT ek field hai POORE POST par, per channel nahi. Agar twitter ko ek baar provider ne already dekh liya hai (chahe woh attempt fail hua ho), toh us provider ka 'seen' hona un-see nahi ho sakta. Ek post jiske 2 channels hain -- ek already attempted, ek abhi fresh -- agar edit allow kare, toh content badal jaayega aur jo channel already attempted tha usne PURANA content dekha tha, naya channel NAYA content dekhega. Yeh half-edited state hai jisko express karne ka koi tarika nahi hai single `content` field mein.

Isliye editPost loop karta hai har non-canceled delivery par: `if (delivery.attempts > 0) throw POST_ALREADY_DISPATCHED`. Canceled channel ko skip kiya jaata hai kyunki woh future mein kuch dekhega hi nahi -- uska attempts count matter hi nahi karta.
why_needed: Interviewer samajhna chahta hai ki candidate 'what can be undone vs what cannot' ka distinction samajhta hai, aur single-field-vs-per-field content design ka implication.
real_world_analogy: Ek letter jo abhi post nahi hui, use rewrite karna easy hai. Par ek letter jiska ek copy already kisi ko bheja gaya hai, uska content badalna matlab ab do log do alag versions dekhenge -- dono copies ko sync rakhna impossible hai bina dono ko wapas mangaye.
how_it_works: cancelChannel/cancelPost: delivery.status === 'pending' hi kaafi hai. editPost: har non-canceled delivery.attempts === 0 zaroori hai, nahi toh POST_ALREADY_DISPATCHED.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ke cancelChannel, cancelPost aur editPost methods; test/cancel-edit.test.ts ka 'rejects editing a post once ANY channel has been attempted, even if that channel is still pending (mid-retry)'.
advantages: Content consistency guaranteed -- koi channel kabhi mismatched content nahi dekhega
Cancel remains flexible -- mid-retry bhi cancel ho sakta hai, no wasted provider calls prevented from stopping
disadvantages: Ek single channel ka ek attempt poore post ka edit lock kar deta hai, chahe doosre channels abhi fresh hon
Caller ko workaround karna padta hai: pehle attempted channel cancel karo, phir edit karo
common_mistakes: Cancel aur edit ko same rule maan lena -- dono 'pending' check karte hain par different depth par
Canceled channel ko bhi attempts>0 check mein include karna, jo valid edit scenarios ko galat block kar deta
follow_up_questions: If content became per-channel instead of per-post, how would editPost's restriction change?
Why does canceling an attempted channel BEFORE editing unlock the edit for the rest of the post?

question: Stage 1 had no retryable-vs-permanent distinction -- every provider failure retried until maxAttempts. Stage 2 added an optional retryable flag. Why was it deferred to stage 2, and why is it optional here when project 21's SendResult.retryable is required?
answer_hinglish:
Stage 1 mein yeh ek deliberate scope cut tha: har failure, chahe 'instance down' (temporary) ho ya 'invalid token' (permanent), ek hi path se guzarti thi -- backoff ke saath maxAttempts tak retry, phir dead_letter. Pehle core (fan-out, idempotency, dispatching guard) solid karna zyada important tha, aur PLAN.md ne isko 'one more field on ProviderResult, not a redesign' bola tha. Stage 2 ne exactly wahi kiya: ProviderResult ke failed variant mein `retryable?: boolean`.

Ab optional kyun, jabki project 21 ka `SendResult.retryable` REQUIRED hai? Project 21 mein har sender shuru se hi yeh decide karne ke liye likha gaya tha, toh required field ka koi cost nahi tha. Yahan stage 1 already teen fake providers aur callers ship kar chuka tha jo `{ status: "failed", reason }` return karte hain, bina retryable key ke. Required banane ka matlab ek breaking type change -- har provider ko touch karna. Optional + explicit rule 'absent matlab retryable' se har stage-1 failure path EXACTLY pehle jaisa behave karta hai, zero code change. Isliye dispatchChannel `result.retryable === false` check karta hai -- sirf explicit false permanent hai.

Cost yeh hai ki type system tumhe decide karne ke liye force nahi karta: ek naya real provider jo auth failure par flag set karna bhool jaaye, silently retry karta rahega. Par woh 'safe' default hai -- zyada retries, kabhi galat early dead-letter nahi -- isliye yeh trade acceptable hai.
why_needed: Interviewer check karta hai ki tum 'same field, alag project, alag decision' ko context se justify kar sakte ho -- backward compatibility vs type-level strictness ka trade-off, sirf 'project 21 mein required tha toh yahan bhi hona chahiye' nahi.
real_world_analogy: Ek office ke form mein naya field 'urgent?' add hua. Purane forms jinme yeh field hai hi nahi, unhe 'not urgent' maan lo -- warna har purana form reject karna padega. Naye department (project 21) ne shuru se hi field mandatory rakha, kyunki unke paas koi purane forms the hi nahi.
how_it_works: src/types.ts: `{ status: "failed"; reason: string; retryable?: boolean }`. src/scheduler.ts dispatchChannel ka failure branch: `const permanent = result.retryable === false; if (permanent || delivery.attempts >= delivery.maxAttempts) dead_letter; else nextAttemptAt = now + backoffMs(...)`. Provider-throws wala catch path ek result banata hai jisme retryable key hoti hi nahi, isliye ek throw retryable rehta hai -- project 21 ka bhi yahi rule hai.
in_this_project: PLAN.md 'Stage 2 decisions' ka pehla bullet yeh poori reasoning likhta hai. src/types.ts mein ProviderResult ke upar comment: 'optional here (instead of required there) specifically so stage 1's existing ProviderResult-returning code needs no changes'. Contrast: projects/21-notification/src/types.ts mein `retryable: boolean` required hai. Backward compat ka evidence: stage 1 ke 84 tests unmodified pass hue (ab total 90), aur mutation R9 (AlwaysFailsProvider ka default false kar do) ne 12 stage-1 tests tod diye.
advantages: Zero changes to stage 1 providers and call sites -- every old failure stays retryable
Safe default: a forgotten flag means extra retries, never a wrongly early dead_letter
Same name and meaning as project 21, so the concept transfers across the repo
disadvantages: The type system does not force a new provider to classify its failures, unlike project 21's required field
A permanent failure from a provider that forgets the flag still burns the full backoff schedule before dead-lettering
common_mistakes: Checking `!result.retryable` -- with an optional field, undefined is falsy and every stage 1 failure would turn permanent
Treating optional-vs-required as a style choice; here it is a backward-compatibility decision forced by already-shipped providers
Forgetting that the provider-throws catch path must also stay retryable
follow_up_questions: Would you ever migrate retryable to required here, and how would you roll that out?
Why does a provider that throws stay retryable instead of being treated as permanent?
How would an operator tell 'dead-lettered by a permanent failure' from 'exhausted retries'?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Required field = compile-time guarantee ki har provider ne socha, par breaking change. Optional + 'absent = retryable' = zero migration, par guarantee sirf ek runtime convention hai. Is project mein providers fake aur gine-chune hain, isliye compatibility jeeti; ek bade real-provider codebase mein phased approach (pehle optional, phir required) behtar hoga.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Ek real provider jo revoked OAuth token par retryable omit kare, poora maxAttempts * backoff time waste karega aur channel 'pending' dikhta rahega jabki woh actually hopeless hai. Ulta, ek provider jo transient 503 ko retryable: false bol de, ek recoverable post ko attempt 1 par dead-letter kar dega -- scheduler provider ke classification par poora trust karta hai.
advanced.alternatives: Project 21 jaisa required boolean; ek enum taxonomy (transient/permanent/unknown); ya classification scheduler ke andar ek pluggable policy function mein (reason/error code dekh kar) -- tab provider ko kuch decide nahi karna padta, par policy ko har platform ke error formats jaanne padte.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Chhote scale par fark minor hai. 100x par, agar ek shared OAuth integration revoke ho jaaye aur hazaaron channels us par hon, flag ke bina sab maxAttempts tak retry karte -- provider quota aur tick() ka scan dono waste. Flag ke saath woh ek hi attempt mein terminal ho jaate hain.
advanced.production_improvements: lastError ke saath ek structured cause (jaise deadLetterCause: 'permanent' | 'exhausted') store karna, permanent dead-letters par alag alert, aur real providers mein platform error codes -> retryable mapping ko contract tests se pin karna. Yeh sab is project mein abhi nahi hai.

question: Why does schedulePost's idempotency check-then-set need no synchronous claim, unlike project 22 (messaging) stage 2's placeholder claim?
answer_hinglish:
Yeh PLAN.md ka sabse deliberately-contrasted decision hai. Project 22 (messaging) stage 2 mein, send/deliver jaise operations ke beech mein ek REAL `await` tha commit se pehle -- matlab do truly concurrent calls same clientRequestId ke saath dono await ke PEHLE map check kar sakte the (dono ko lagta 'yeh naya hai'), aur dono apna commit kar dete, duplicate records ban jaate. Isliye ek synchronous PLACEHOLDER claim (`pendingOps` jaisa) zaroori thi check aur commit ke beech mein 'yeh request already claim ho gaya hai' bolne ke liye.

Is project mein, `schedulePost()` POORA synchronous hai -- validation, idempotency map check, record build, map set -- koi await kahin bhi nahi hai is poore path mein. JavaScript ek function body ko EK turn mein chalata hai (single-threaded event loop) -- matlab jab tak `schedulePost()` ka pehla call `return` nahi karta, uska code kabhi 'pause' nahi hota taaki doosra call beech mein shuru ho sake. Isliye doosra `schedulePost()` call, SAME clientRequestId ke saath, ONLY tab start ho sakta hai jab pehla call already return kar chuka ho -- aur us waqt tak idempotency key already map mein set ho chuki hai.

Yeh deliberate hai, oversight nahi -- `tick()` hi is project ka EK jagah hai jahan await hota hai, aur tick() scheduling path par kahin nahi hai.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate samajhta hai JavaScript ke single-threaded run-to-completion model ka exact implication concurrency safety par, aur yeh bhi ki yeh guarantee TABHI tak valid hai jab tak code truly synchronous rahe.
real_world_analogy: Ek clerk jo pura form EK saans mein fill karta hai bina kahin rukne ke -- usse pehle woh form complete na kar le, doosra customer line mein kabhi uski jagah nahi le sakta. Par agar woh form fill karte-karte ek baar coffee break le (await), tab doosra customer uski jagah aa sakta hai aur confusion ho sakta hai.
how_it_works: schedulePost: requireClientRequestId -> idempotency.get() check -> (if new) validate content/channels/scheduledAt -> build record -> posts.set() + idempotency.set(). Koi await kahin nahi, isliye 'check then set' hi dedupe ke liye enough hai.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka schedulePost method -- poora method body mein koi `await` keyword hi nahi hai. Contrast: projects/22-messaging/src/messenger.ts ka claimOp/pendingOps pattern, jo waha zaroori hai kyunki wahan async commit path hai.
advantages: No extra placeholder/claim bookkeeping needed -- simpler code
No risk of a claim being left behind if something throws mid-commit (nothing is 'half-committed' since there's no await to interleave)
disadvantages: This guarantee breaks the moment ANY await is introduced on the scheduling path -- fragile to a future refactor
A reader unfamiliar with JS's run-to-completion model might assume a race exists and add unnecessary locking
common_mistakes: Adding an await to schedulePost (e.g. for a future real DB write) without also adding back a synchronous claim
Assuming this synchronous-safety argument applies to tick(), which DOES await provider.send()
follow_up_questions: If schedulePost() someday needed to await a real database write before committing, what would break, and what would you add back?
Why is this argument specific to JavaScript's concurrency model and would not hold in a genuinely multi-threaded language?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Synchronous-only scheduling path ek strong simplicity win hai, par yeh ek IMPLICIT invariant hai jo code review discipline par depend karta hai -- koi automated check nahi rokta kisi future developer ko ek await add karne se bina claim wapas laaye.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar koi future change schedulePost mein ek await daal de (jaise ek real persistence call) bina synchronous claim wapas laaye, toh N truly-concurrent calls same clientRequestId ke saath N duplicate posts bana sakte hain -- exactly woh bug jo messaging stage 2 explicitly guard karta hai.
advanced.alternatives: Hamesha ek synchronous claim pattern use karna (messaging ka pendingOps jaisa) chahe abhi zaroorat na ho, taaki future-proof rahe -- par yeh is stage ke liye unnecessary complexity hoti, jab koi await hi nahi hai.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Yeh guarantee scale-independent hai (single process ke andar) -- 10x ya 100x calls bhi is same single-threaded run-to-completion rule follow karte hain. Jo scale IMPACT karta hai woh multi-PROCESS deployment hai, jahan har process ka apna idempotency Map hoga -- shared storage (Redis/DB) chahiye hoga cross-process dedupe ke liye.
advanced.production_improvements: Jab bhi schedulePost real persistence add kare, PEHLE yeh decide karna ki woh persistence synchronous rahegi (in-memory ki tarah) ya async -- agar async, messaging stage 2 ka claim pattern seedha reuse karna, redesign nahi.

question: Why does each post fan out to one independent ChannelDelivery per channel instead of keeping a single status field on the post as a whole?
answer_hinglish:
README/PLAN.md dono isi reasoning use karte hain jo project 22 (messaging) ke per-recipient receipts use karta hai: 'delivered' ek property hai (post, channel) PAIR ki, sirf post ki nahi. Agar poore post par ek single status hota, toh ek sawal hamesha ambiguous rehta -- agar linkedin sent ho gaya par twitter abhi retry kar raha hai, poore post ka status kya kahoge? 'Partially sent'? Yeh ek naya status value banana padta jo khud bahut kam information deta (kaunsa channel sent hua, kaunsa nahi, yeh abhi bhi alag se track karna padta).

Per-channel fan-out mein yeh ambiguity hi exist nahi karti -- har channel independently apna status, attempts, nextAttemptAt, aur terminal fields (providerId/sentAt ya lastError) carry karta hai. Post-level koi aggregate status nahi hai; caller ko simply `post.deliveries` ke through har channel dekhna hota hai.

Yeh independence sirf STORAGE mein nahi, BEHAVIOR mein bhi guarantee hoti hai: ek channel ka provider fail/throw/dead-letter kabhi doosre channel ke counters ya status ko touch nahi karta -- dedicated tests (jaise tick.test.ts ka 'per-channel independence' describe block) isko directly assert karte hain, do providers ke beech.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate 'granularity of state' ka sahi level pick karna samajhta hai -- jab ek entity ka outcome actually kayi independent sub-entities ka outcome hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek courier jo ek hi shipment mein 3 alag packages 3 alag addresses par bhej raha ho -- har package ka apna tracking status hota hai, poori shipment ka koi single 'delivered' ya 'not delivered' status nahi ho sakta jab tak sab packages terminal na ho jaayein.
how_it_works: ScheduledPost.deliveries: Record<string, ChannelDelivery>. Har channel ki apni independent status/attempts/nextAttemptAt/providerId/lastError/sentAt/canceledAt fields hoti hain.
in_this_project: src/types.ts ka ScheduledPost.deliveries aur ChannelDelivery; test/tick.test.ts ka 'per-channel independence' describe block jo 2 providers ke beech counters ko assert karta hai.
advantages: No ambiguous aggregate status -- each channel's truth is explicit
A failing channel never masks or corrupts a sibling's state
Natural to extend: adding a channel is just adding another entry in the deliveries map
disadvantages: Caller must iterate deliveries themselves to answer 'is this post fully done' -- there is no single convenience field
A post targeting many channels has proportionally more state to inspect
common_mistakes: Trying to derive a single post-level status and caching it, which then needs to be kept in sync with every channel change
Assuming one channel's retry count affects a sibling's -- the tests exist specifically to disprove this
follow_up_questions: If a post targets 100 channels, at what point does a plain object keyed by channel stop being the right data structure?
How would you compute a derived 'overall post status' for a UI without storing it as mutable state?

question: What is missing from this project before it could actually schedule real posts to real social platforms?
answer_hinglish:
Sabse pehla aur sabse bada gap: REAL provider implementations. Abhi `FakeChannelProvider` interface ko sirf `AlwaysSucceedsProvider`/`AlwaysFailsProvider`/`FlakyProvider` implement karte hain -- koi inme se kabhi real LinkedIn/Twitter/Mastodon API call nahi karta. Production mein har platform ke liye ek real provider likhna padega jo unke actual REST/GraphQL APIs call kare.

Uske saath hi OAuth zaroori hai -- har social platform apne account ko access karne ke liye OAuth token maangta hai, aur woh tokens EXPIRE hote hain, refresh karne padte hain. Abhi iska koi trace nahi hai is project mein -- FakeChannelProvider ka `send()` kabhi kisi credential ki parwaah nahi karta.

Teesra: per-channel content length rules. Abhi `MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH = 2000` HAR channel ke liye same hai, par Twitter ka limit ~280 characters hai, LinkedIn ka ~3000 -- ek post jo linkedin ke liye theek hai woh twitter ko bhejne par turant reject ho sakta hai REAL platform se, jo abhi is project mein kabhi nahi hoga kyunki fake providers content length check hi nahi karte.

Chautha: `tick()` abhi polled hai, ek single in-process caller ke through -- real deployment mein multiple workers chahiye honge throughput ke liye, jiske liye project 21 jaisa job queue with leases zaroori hoga, idempotency key expiry (abhi keys kabhi expire nahi hote, memory grow karti hai), aur ek HTTP/worker layer jo abhi exist hi nahi karti.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate ek 'fake provider, in-memory' prototype aur ek real production system ke beech ka GAP identify kar sakta hai, specifically is codebase ke context mein.
real_world_analogy: Ek demo app jo screenshot dikhata hai 'email sent!' bina kabhi real SMTP server ko touch kiye -- woh demo kaam karta hai, par production mein actual email provider, credentials, retry policy, aur rate limits sab chahiye honge.
how_it_works: FakeChannelProvider interface already abstraction hai jahan real providers plug ho sakte hain -- scheduler khud kabhi nahi badalna padega, sirf naya class likhna hoga jo FakeChannelProvider implement kare real API calls ke saath.
in_this_project: src/providers.ts ka FakeChannelProvider interface aur teen fake implementations; src/scheduler.ts ka MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH constant (single, not per-channel).
advantages: FakeChannelProvider interface already provides the right seam -- real providers can be dropped in without touching SocialScheduler
The fake-provider test suite (providers/tick/cancel-edit) gives confidence the orchestration logic is correct before real integrations are added
disadvantages: Real providers introduce network latency, rate limits, and partial failures the fake providers never model
OAuth token lifecycle management is a whole additional subsystem not represented anywhere in this project today
common_mistakes: Assuming the orchestration logic (retry/backoff/dead-letter) needs to change for real providers -- it does not, only the provider implementations do
Forgetting per-channel content limits until a real post gets rejected by a real platform
follow_up_questions: How would you design a real LinkedinProvider that implements FakeChannelProvider's send() signature?
Where would OAuth token refresh logic live -- inside the provider, or as a separate concern the scheduler is unaware of?
What would need to change in schedulePost's validation to support per-channel content limits?

question: How would you add per-channel content length rules (Twitter's ~280 characters vs LinkedIn's ~3000) to this project?
answer_hinglish:
Abhi `requireContent` sirf EK global check karta hai: `content.length > MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH` (2000). Yeh check `schedulePost`/`editPost` dono mein, VALIDATION time par hota hai, channel-specific nahi -- content ek single string hai poore post ke liye, channels sirf ek list hain.

Per-channel limits add karne ke liye sabse pehla sawal yeh hai: content TOH ek field hai poore post par (jaisa SOC-104/107 mein discuss hua), toh ek hi content string ko ALAG-ALAG limits ke against kaise check karoge? Simplest approach: schedulePost validation mein, har channel ke liye ek `CHANNEL_LIMITS: Record<string, number>` config dekho, aur `content.length` ko SABSE CHHOTE applicable limit ke against check karo (jo channels is post mein target kiye gaye hain) -- taaki jo bhi content accept ho, woh HAR target channel ke liye valid ho.

Iska downside yeh hai ki agar koi post sirf linkedin (3000 limit) target kare, uska content bhi 280 se bada nahi ho sakta agar validation 'minimum of all registered channels' use kare instead of 'minimum of THIS post's channels' -- isliye sahi design woh hai jo sirf is specific schedulePost call ke `request.channels` ko dekhe, poore providers map ko nahi.

Ek alternative (zyada flexible, zyada complex): per-channel content override allow karna -- post ka ek base content ho, aur optionally per-channel override. Yeh scope creep hai is stage ke liye; PLAN.md explicitly 'one content length limit for every channel' ko current scope ke andar hi rakhta hai.
why_needed: Interviewer yeh dekhna chahta hai ki candidate 'single content field + multiple target constraints' ka validation design kar sakta hai, aur per-post vs per-provider scope ka difference samajhta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek hi speech jo tum alag-alag venues mein doge -- agar ek venue ka time-limit 2 minute hai aur doosre ka 10 minute, tumhe apni speech itni chhoti rakhni padegi ki SABSE CHHOTE venue mein bhi fit ho jaaye, warna har venue ke liye alag speech likhni padegi.
how_it_works: Proposed: har channel ke liye ek max-length config maintain karo (provider-level ya constructor option). schedulePost ke requireContent mein, is post ke target channels ke limits ka MINIMUM lo, aur content ko uske against check karo.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka requireContent (current single MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH check) aur requireValidChannels (jahan channel list already iterate hoti hai validation ke dauraan).
advantages: A single content field stays simple to reason about -- no per-channel override complexity
Catches an unpostable-on-one-channel post at request time, before any channel ever dispatches
disadvantages: A post targeting Twitter and LinkedIn together is forced down to Twitter's tighter limit even for LinkedIn's delivery
Does not let a caller write a longer LinkedIn-specific version and a shorter Twitter-specific one in the same post
common_mistakes: Checking content length against the minimum limit across ALL registered providers instead of just this post's target channels
Forgetting to apply the same per-channel check inside editPost's content validation, not just schedulePost's
follow_up_questions: How would per-channel content overrides change the ScheduledPost and ChannelDelivery types?
Where should the CHANNEL_LIMITS config live -- hardcoded, a constructor option, or a property the provider itself exposes?

question: A marketing team wants multiple worker processes dispatching due posts concurrently for higher throughput. What has to change?
answer_hinglish:
Abhi `tick()` ek single-caller model assume karta hai -- `dispatching` Set sirf SAME caller ke apne overlap (slow provider + doosra tick() call) ke against protect karta hai. Agar DO ALAG processes same scheduler instance (ya worse, alag in-memory instances) par tick() call karein, do problems aayenge: (1) agar woh same in-memory SocialScheduler object share kar rahe hain, `dispatching` Set abhi bhi kaam karega kyunki JS single-threaded hai -- par yeh in-process multi-worker scenario hai, real multi-PROCESS nahi. (2) Agar har process ka apna ALAG SocialScheduler instance hai (jo horizontal scaling mein normal hai), har process ka apna `posts` Map, apna `idempotency` Map, apna `dispatching` Set hoga -- koi coordination nahi, SAME due channel do processes se dobara dispatch ho sakta hai.

Real fix: PLAN.md khud point karta hai project 21 (notification) stage 2 ki taraf -- ek lease-based job queue (`InMemoryJobQueue` jaisa, par real deployment mein ek shared backend jaisa Postgres `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` ya Redis). Har due channel ek 'job' ban jaata, ek worker usse `claim(now, max, leaseMs)` karta -- ek `leaseToken` milta hai, aur sirf WOHI token wala worker `complete`/`reschedule` kar sakta hai. Agar worker crash ho jaaye lease expire hone se pehle commit kiye bina, job automatically visible ho jaata hai doosre worker ke liye.

Saath hi, `posts`/`idempotency`/`dispatching` sab ek SHARED durable store mein jaana chahiye (abhi sab in-memory Maps hain, per-process) -- nahi toh workers ek doosre ki state dekh hi nahi payenge.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate single-process polling se multi-worker distributed dispatch tak scale karne ka poora path samajhta hai, aur existing codebase (project 21) ka reference kar sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek hi restaurant mein ek waiter sab orders khud track karta hai apne notepad par -- yeh kaam karta hai jab tak sirf ek waiter hai. Jaise hi 5 waiters ek saath kaam karte hain, sabko ek SHARED order board chahiye jahan ek order EK hi waiter ko assign ho, aur agar woh waiter busy ho jaaye, kisi aur ko mil sake.
how_it_works: Each due channel becomes a claimable job (postId:channel). A worker calls claim(), gets a leaseToken, dispatches, then complete()/reschedule(). Shared state (posts, idempotency, the job queue itself) must live in a backend all worker processes can see.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts's current in-process dispatching Set and tick(); project 21's src/queue.ts (JobQueue interface, InMemoryJobQueue) and src/worker.ts are the reusable reference design named in PLAN.md.
advantages: A lease-based queue lets throughput scale roughly linearly with worker count (within the backend's capacity)
Project 21's design is already built and tested -- this is reuse, not a from-scratch design
disadvantages: Requires a shared durable backend (DB/Redis) instead of in-memory Maps -- a real infrastructure dependency
Lease tuning (leaseMs too short re-claims live work, too long delays recovery from a dead worker) becomes an operational concern
common_mistakes: Running multiple workers against separate in-memory SocialScheduler instances and assuming the dispatching Set protects across processes -- it does not, it is per-instance
Forgetting that posts/idempotency also need to be shared, not just the job queue
follow_up_questions: What happens to a channel's attempts counter if a worker claims it, starts dispatching, then crashes before completing?
How would you size leaseMs relative to how long a real provider's send() call might take?
What would the migration path look like from today's in-memory tick() to this design, without a full rewrite?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Moving to a lease-based job queue trades today's zero-infrastructure simplicity (in-memory Maps/Set) for a real shared backend dependency -- a necessary trade the moment more than one process needs to drive dispatch, but not free: every operation that used to be a plain Map lookup becomes a network call.
advanced.failure_scenarios: A worker that claims a job, calls provider.send(), then crashes before calling complete() leaves the job claimed until its lease expires -- during that window the channel is neither dispatched again nor visibly stuck, which could look like a silent delay to monitoring unless lease-expiry events are also tracked.
advanced.alternatives: A fully external managed queue (SQS, Pub/Sub) instead of a custom lease table; or sharding posts across workers by postId hash so each worker owns a disjoint subset with no claiming needed at all, trading dynamic load-balancing for simplicity.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At 10x throughput needs, a handful of workers against a shared InMemoryJobQueue-style backend is enough. At 100x, the backend itself (claim()'s scan, lock contention) becomes the bottleneck, pushing toward a database-indexed or broker-backed queue instead of a simple shared table.
advanced.production_improvements: Reuse project 21's JobQueue interface and InMemoryJobQueue as the starting contract, swap its backing store for a durable one (Postgres SKIP LOCKED or Redis) before going multi-process, and add lease-expiry monitoring so a crashed worker's stuck claim is visible, not silent.

question: What would you monitor in production to catch a channel that's quietly dead-lettering more than it should?
answer_hinglish:
Sabse direct metric: DEAD-LETTER RATE PER CHANNEL -- har channel ke liye, kitne percent delivery attempts `dead_letter` par khatam hue, ek rolling window (jaise last 1 hour) mein. Is project mein `ChannelDelivery.status === "dead_letter"` aur `lastError` already available hai har delivery record par -- ek monitoring layer `scheduler.list()` ko poll kar sakta hai (ya events emit karne ka mechanism add kiya ja sakta hai dispatchChannel mein) aur per-channel count nikal sakta hai.

Ek acha threshold: agar ek specific channel ka dead-letter rate baaki channels se SIGNIFICANTLY zyada hai (jaise linkedin 1% par hai par mastodon 40% par), yeh ek strong signal hai ki us channel ka PROVIDER problem hai -- shayad token expire ho gaya, shayad rate-limited ho raha hai, shayad instance down hai -- is project ke context mein, `lastError` string isi reason ko already carry karta hai diagnostics ke liye.

Doosra complementary metric: AVERAGE ATTEMPTS-TO-SUCCESS per channel. Agar ek channel consistently `attempts=1` par sent ho raha hai, woh healthy hai. Agar average attempts 3-4 ke close pahunch raha hai (maxAttempts ke close), yeh channel 'almost dead-lettering' zone mein hai -- ek EARLY WARNING signal dead-letter rate spike hone se PEHLE.

Teesra: BACKLOG size -- kitne channels abhi `pending` aur `nextAttemptAt <= now` hain (due but undispatched) -- agar yeh number badh raha hai, matlab tick() itni frequently nahi chal rahi ya throughput kaafi nahi hai.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate per-channel observability design kar sakta hai existing data model (status, attempts, lastError) ka use karke, bina naya infrastructure invent kiye.
real_world_analogy: Ek call center jahan har agent ka apna 'dropped call rate' track hota hai -- agar ek agent ka rate suddenly spike kare baaki sabse zyada, supervisor usi agent ki line check karega, poore call center ko nahi.
how_it_works: Poll (or event-hook) scheduler.list(), aggregate deliveries by channel: count of dead_letter / total terminal (sent + dead_letter) over a time window = dead-letter rate. Sum of attempts for sent deliveries / count of sent = average attempts-to-success.
in_this_project: src/types.ts ka ChannelDelivery (status, attempts, lastError fields already present); src/scheduler.ts ka list() method jo saare posts snapshot deta hai.
advantages: Uses data already on ChannelDelivery -- no new fields or events strictly required to get started
Per-channel granularity immediately isolates which integration is unhealthy
disadvantages: Polling scheduler.list() repeatedly over many posts is O(n) each time -- a real deployment would want this emitted as events instead
A rolling window needs its own time-series storage; this project has no built-in metrics emission
common_mistakes: Looking only at an aggregate dead-letter rate across all channels, which hides one badly-behaving channel among many healthy ones
Alerting only on dead_letter count instead of a RATE, which doesn't account for traffic volume differences between channels
follow_up_questions: How would you turn this polling-based metric into an event-driven one without changing tick()'s public signature?
What would you alert on first: a dead-letter rate spike, or a rising average-attempts-to-success trend?

question: What would you check first if an on-call engineer gets paged 'posts aren't going out'?
answer_hinglish:
Sabse pehla sawal: tick() CALL ho raha hai ya nahi? Yeh project bilkul explicitly 'tick() is polled' hai -- koi internal scheduler loop nahi hai (README mein likha hai, project 21's flushDue() jaisa). Agar caller ne tick() ko call karna ROKH diya (cron job down, worker process crashed), koi post kabhi dispatch nahi hoga chahe scheduler ka internal state bilkul healthy ho. Yeh sabse common aur sabse boring cause hota hai production mein.

Doosra check: due-but-undispatched BACKLOG kitna bada hai -- `pending` status wale channels jinka `nextAttemptAt <= now`. Agar backlog grow kar raha hai (tick() chal raha hai par posts accumulate ho rahe hain), matlab tick() ki FREQUENCY kaafi nahi hai load ke against, ya ek specific tick() call fail/hang ho rahi hai.

Teesra: kya saare posts affected hain ya sirf ek CHANNEL? Agar sirf ek channel (jaise mastodon) stuck hai aur baaki (linkedin/twitter) normally dispatch ho rahe hain, problem us specific provider mein hai (dead letters, ya provider.send() hang ho raha hai) -- `dispatching` guard set check karo: agar koi `postId:channel` key permanently stuck reh gayi hai (jo ek bug hoga -- `finally` block mein `dispatching.delete()` guaranteed hona chahiye), woh channel kabhi phir se claimed nahi hoga.

Chautha: clock drift -- agar is deployment mein `systemClock` use ho raha hai aur server ka system time galat set hai, `scheduledAt`/`nextAttemptAt` comparisons galat result de sakte hain.
why_needed: Interviewer ek realistic on-call debugging checklist expect karta hai, is specific project ke actual mechanisms (polled tick, dispatching guard, per-channel independence) ke against grounded.
real_world_analogy: Ek factory assembly line jahan koi worker kabhi machine ka start button nahi dabata -- machine khud bilkul theek hai, bas koi usse chalaa hi nahi raha. Pehla check hamesha yeh hona chahiye ki machine chalaayi gayi thi ya nahi, phir machine ke andar jaake dekhna chahiye.
how_it_works: Check: (1) is tick() being invoked at all, (2) due-but-pending backlog size and trend, (3) is the stall isolated to one channel/provider, (4) clock correctness. Each maps to a distinct known failure mode in this project's design.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka tick() (the only dispatch entrypoint) aur dispatching Set (should never leak a stuck key thanks to the try/finally in dispatchChannel).
advantages: Each check maps directly to a known, documented mechanism in this project -- no guesswork needed
The checks are ordered cheapest-and-most-likely-first (is tick even running?) before deeper state inspection
disadvantages: Without added monitoring (SOC-111/113), several of these checks require manually inspecting scheduler.list() rather than a dashboard
A stuck dispatching key due to a real bug would be very hard to detect without inspecting the Set directly, since it is private
common_mistakes: Jumping straight to 'the provider must be down' before confirming tick() is even being called
Treating a single-channel stall as a whole-system outage instead of checking per-channel independence first
follow_up_questions: How would you expose the dispatching Set's size or contents for debugging without making it part of the public API?
What would make you suspect a clock problem specifically, versus a tick()-not-running problem?

question: How would you monitor the backlog of due-but-undispatched channels, and what would you alert on?
answer_hinglish:
Backlog ka definition yahan precise hai: woh channels jinka `status === "pending"` AND `nextAttemptAt <= now` -- matlab woh dispatch ho jaane CHAHIYE the par abhi tak nahi hue (ya toh tick() nahi chala, ya `dispatching` guard ne unhe skip kiya pichhle call mein). Yeh backlog size ek SINGLE number hai jo poore system ki dispatch-health ko summarize karta hai.

Computation: `scheduler.list()` se saare posts lo, har delivery check karo `status === 'pending' && nextAttemptAt <= clock.now()`. Is project mein koi built-in metric emitter nahi hai, isliye production mein yeh ek periodic job hoga jo scheduler state snapshot leta hai (ya better, tick() ke return value -- jo 'count of attempts made this call' deta hai -- ko ek counter mein track karta hai, plus ek ALAG query jo backlog size directly measure kare).

Alerting strategy: ABSOLUTE size se zyada important hai TREND aur AGE. Ek backlog of 50 channels normal ho sakta hai agar woh hamesha turant clear ho jaata hai next tick() par. Par agar backlog GROW kar raha hai consistently (tick() rate se zyada tezi se naye due channels aa rahe hain), ya agar koi channel backlog mein LAMBE time se (jaise 10+ minutes se due) hai, yeh dono clear signals hain ki dispatch throughput kaafi nahi hai ya kuch stuck hai.

Ek additional refinement: backlog ko PER-CHANNEL bhi track karna -- agar sirf ek channel ka backlog badh raha hai (baaki clear ho rahe hain), problem us specific provider mein hai, poore tick() mechanism mein nahi.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate throughput-health metrics design kar sakta hai aur trend/age ko absolute count se zyada important samajhta hai alerting ke liye.
real_world_analogy: Ek airport ki security line -- line ki length khud itni problem nahi jitna yeh ki line KITNI DER se badh rahi hai ya koi passenger line mein 30 minute se zyada waqt se khada hai. Ek line jo turant clear ho jaati hai woh fine hai, chahe woh lambi dikh rahi ho.
how_it_works: backlogSize = count of channels where status==pending and nextAttemptAt<=now. Track this over time (trend) and separately track max(now - nextAttemptAt) across those channels (age/staleness) for the oldest stuck one.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka tick() internal due-detection logic (same filter, exposed read-only for monitoring) and ChannelDelivery.nextAttemptAt.
advantages: Directly derived from existing fields -- no schema change needed to start measuring this
Separating trend/age from raw count avoids false alarms on a naturally-bursty but healthy backlog
disadvantages: Computing this by scanning every post (O(n)) does not scale well without an index by nextAttemptAt as post volume grows
No built-in event hook in this project -- monitoring has to poll externally
common_mistakes: Alerting on raw backlog count alone without considering normal traffic bursts
Not distinguishing a backlog that clears within one tick() cycle from one that keeps growing cycle over cycle
follow_up_questions: What data structure change would make computing this backlog cheaper than an O(n) scan over every post?
How would you turn tick()'s return value (count of channel-attempts made) into a throughput metric alongside this backlog metric?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Computing backlog by scanning scheduler.list() is the simplest possible implementation and needs zero schema changes, but it couples monitoring cost directly to total post volume rather than to backlog size itself -- an architecture with a proper due-time index would decouple the two.
advanced.failure_scenarios: A slow but steady backlog growth (tick() running, but at a rate slightly below incoming due-channel rate) is easy to miss with a simple threshold alert, since the backlog may stay under any fixed number for a long time before suddenly becoming large -- a trend-based alert (rate of change) catches this far earlier than an absolute-size alert.
advanced.alternatives: Emit a backlog-size event directly from inside tick() itself (computed once per call as a byproduct of the existing scan, nearly free) instead of a separate external polling job that re-scans everything; or maintain a running due-count incrementally as deliveries transition status, avoiding full rescans entirely.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At 10x post volume, the O(n) scan-based backlog check is still cheap enough to run every few seconds. At 100x+, re-scanning every post purely for monitoring becomes a meaningful tax on top of tick()'s own scan cost (SOC-114) -- at that point, deriving the metric from tick()'s own pass (rather than a separate scan) becomes worth the refactor.
advanced.production_improvements: Have tick() itself emit {due: due.length, oldestStaleMs} as part of its return/telemetry instead of relying on an external poll that duplicates the scan. Alert on sustained upward trend over a rolling window and on any single channel's staleness exceeding an SLA threshold, not on raw backlog size alone.

question: A marketing team wants to schedule thousands of posts across hundreds of channels for a product launch. What in this project's current design would fall over first, and how would you plan capacity around it?
answer_hinglish:
Pehla bottleneck: `tick()` ka due-detection step `for (const record of this.posts.values()) for (const delivery of Object.values(record.deliveries))` -- yeh HAR post, HAR channel ko scan karta hai HAR tick() call par, chahe woh due ho ya nahi. Thousands of posts x hundreds of channels each matlab lakhon deliveries HAR tick() mein scan ho rahi hain -- yeh O(total deliveries) hai, O(due deliveries) nahi. Jaise volume badhta hai, tick()'s latency badhta jaayega chahe actual due work chhota ho.

Doosra: `providers` map ek fixed set hai -- agar launch mein naye channels (jaise naye regional accounts) dynamically add karna ho, abhi sirf constructor time par providers diye ja sakte hain, runtime par naya provider register karne ka koi method nahi hai.

Teesra: sab kuch ek single in-memory process mein hai -- ek bada launch burst (thousands of posts simultaneously due, jaise sabka `scheduledAt` ek hi campaign-launch-time ho) ek SINGLE tick() call ko bahut saari `Promise.all` dispatches ek saath chalane ke liye force karega -- yeh is project ke current design mein koi concurrency limit nahi hai, matlab ek burst poore event loop ko busy kar sakta hai.

Capacity planning ke liye: (1) ek indexed due-queue (nextAttemptAt se sorted) banana taaki tick() sirf ACTUALLY due channels scan kare, O(n) nahi. (2) tick() ki dispatch batch size limit karna (jaise ek baar mein max 500 channels), taaki ek bada burst poora event loop block na kare. (3) SOC-110 wala multi-worker job queue design, taaki throughput single-process limit se aage badh sake.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate specific implementation details (O(n) scan, Promise.all without a concurrency cap) se real scaling bottleneck identify kar sakta hai, generic answers nahi deta.
real_world_analogy: Ek chhoti reception desk jahan ek person HAR visitor ka naam poore guest-book mein scan karta hai yeh check karne ke liye ki unka appointment abhi hai ya nahi -- yeh fine hai 10 visitors ke liye, par 10,000 visitors ke saath, poora guest-book baar-baar scan karna khud ek bottleneck ban jaata hai.
how_it_works: tick()'s current scan is O(total deliveries across all posts) every call. A burst of simultaneously-due channels is dispatched via a single unbounded Promise.all, with no concurrency cap.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka tick() method -- the full for-loop over this.posts.values() and the unbounded Promise.all(due.map(...)).
advantages: The current O(n) scan is simple and correct for the scale this project targets (stage 1, interview-focused)
Identifying this now, before it is a real bottleneck, is cheap -- the fix is additive (an index, a batch cap), not a rewrite
disadvantages: Without an index, due-detection cost grows linearly with total post volume, not with actual due work
An unbounded Promise.all on a large burst risks exhausting resources (open connections, memory) all at once
common_mistakes: Assuming more frequent tick() calls alone solves a throughput problem, when the scan cost itself is the bottleneck
Launching a huge simultaneous burst (same scheduledAt for thousands of posts) without staggering it, maximizing the worst-case tick() cost
follow_up_questions: What data structure would turn tick()'s due-detection from O(total deliveries) into O(due deliveries)?
How would you stagger a marketing team's bulk scheduledAt values to avoid a single enormous due-burst?
What concurrency cap would you add to tick()'s dispatch step, and how would you choose its value?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Ek sorted due-index (jaise min-heap by nextAttemptAt) tick() ko fast banata hai, par maintain karna costlier hai -- har status transition (cancel, retry-reschedule, dead-letter) ko index update karna padega, jo abhi plain object mutation se zyada complex hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Bina kisi fix ke, ek bada launch burst tick()'s scan cost ko spike karega exactly jab system ki zaroorat sabse zyada ho (launch time) -- worst-case timing ka classic example, jahan monitoring (SOC-113) backlog ek sudden spike dikhayega.
advanced.alternatives: Ek priority-queue/min-heap by nextAttemptAt; ya posts ko channel-wise bucket karna taaki ek channel ka backlog doosre channel ki scan cost ko affect na kare; ya database-backed indexing agar persistence add ho rahi hai (SOC jobs queue design).
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x par current O(n) scan abhi bhi manageable hai (milliseconds). 100x+ (lakhon deliveries) par, scan cost noticeable lag create karega har tick() call mein -- is point par ek indexed due-queue ya database query (SOC-110 ka shared backend) zaroori ban jaata hai.
advanced.production_improvements: Due-detection ko O(due) banane ke liye ek index add karna. tick()'s dispatch batch ko concurrency-capped banana. Bulk-scheduling tools ko staggered scheduledAt suggest karne ke liye guide karna, taaki simultaneous due-bursts avoid ho sakein.

question: Walk through tick()'s exact control flow, from scanning posts to calling a FakeChannelProvider.
answer_hinglish:
`tick()` teen phases mein chalta hai, poore method mein. Phase 1 (scan): `const now = this.clock.now()`, phir DOUBLE for-loop -- `for (const record of this.posts.values())` aur uske andar `for (const delivery of Object.values(record.deliveries))`. Har delivery ke liye check hota hai teen conditions ek saath: `delivery.status === "pending"`, `delivery.nextAttemptAt <= now`, aur `!this.dispatching.has(key)` jahan `key = postId:channel`. Teeno true hone par hi woh `due` array mein push hota hai `{ record, delivery }` ke saath.

Phase 2 (claim): due array ke HAR entry ke liye, `this.dispatching.add(key)` call hota hai -- yeh LOOP hai, saari claims phase 1 scan khatam hone ke BAAD hoti hain, ek saath (synchronously, ek hi for-loop mein, koi await nahi abhi tak).

Phase 3 (dispatch): `await Promise.all(due.map(({ record, delivery }) => this.dispatchChannel(record, delivery)))` -- yeh SAARE claimed channels ko PARALLEL dispatch karta hai. `dispatchChannel` private method hai: `delivery.attempts += 1` (SYNCHRONOUS, await se pehle), phir `provider.send({...})` await hota hai try/catch ke andar (throw bhi 'failed' treat hota hai), phir result ke hisaab se status/providerId/sentAt ya lastError/nextAttemptAt/dead_letter update hota hai, aur `finally` block mein `this.dispatching.delete(key)` GUARANTEED chalta hai.

`tick()` return karta hai `due.length` -- kitne channel-attempts is call mein hue.
why_needed: Interviewer exact code-trace expect karta hai, line-by-line, is method ko samajhne ke liye kitni depth tak -- yeh dekhne ke liye ki candidate ne sirf docs nahi, actual code pada hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek kitchen order system -- pehle saare pending orders dekho jo abhi ready-to-cook hain (scan), phir unhe ek chef ko assign karo taaki do chef same order na bana lein (claim), phir sab chefs apna-apna order parallel mein banate hain (dispatch), aur jab koi chef khatam kare, uska naam board se hatao chahe order succeed ho ya fail ho (finally).
how_it_works: Scan (filter pending+due+not-already-dispatching) -> claim (mark dispatching) -> dispatch (Promise.all over dispatchChannel, each with attempts++ before its one await, and a finally that always releases the dispatching claim).
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka tick() method aur private dispatchChannel method -- exact two-phase (scan-then-claim, then dispatch) structure.
advantages: Clear two-phase separation (scan-and-claim fully synchronous, then dispatch) makes the one race window easy to reason about
finally guarantees dispatching never leaks a stuck key even if a provider throws or the whole method is interrupted
disadvantages: The scan is O(total deliveries across all posts), not O(due deliveries) -- see SOC-114
