question: What is the exact formula for backoffMs(attempt), and how is it capped?
answer_hinglish:
Formula hai: `backoffMs(attempt, initialMs, maxMs) = min(maxMs, initialMs * 2^(attempt-1))`. `attempt` yahan `delivery.attempts` hai -- jo value ABHI increment ho chuki hai current attempt ke liye (1 on first try, 2 on first retry, waghera).

Isliye attempt=1 ke baad (pehla attempt fail hua), backoff = `initialMs * 2^0 = initialMs` -- pehla retry delay EXACTLY `initialInitialBackoffMs` hai. attempt=2 ke baad, backoff = `initialMs * 2^1 = 2 * initialMs` -- DOUBLE. attempt=3 ke baad, `4 * initialMs`. Yeh classic EXPONENTIAL backoff hai, base 2 ke saath.

`Math.min(maxMs, ...)` HAR computation mein apply hota hai -- matlab jaise hi `initialMs * 2^(attempt-1)` `maxBackoffMs` se bada ho jaaye, result hamesha `maxBackoffMs` par CAP ho jaata hai, kabhi usse aage nahi badhta chahe attempt kitna bhi bada ho jaaye. Yeh prevent karta hai ki backoff delay HOURS ya DAYS tak na badh jaaye agar `maxAttempts` bahut bada set kiya gaya ho.

`dispatchChannel` mein yeh call hoti hai sirf FAILURE path par: `delivery.nextAttemptAt = now + backoffMs(delivery.attempts, this.initialBackoffMs, this.maxBackoffMs)` -- `now` is `this.clock.now()`, jo FAILURE ke baad liya jaata hai, result ke success/fail check hone ke baad.
why_needed: Interviewer exact formula aur edge-case behavior (capping) check karna chahta hai -- yeh dikhata hai candidate ne implementation detail tak dhyaan diya hai, sirf high-level concept nahi.
real_world_analogy: Ek speed limit sign -- koi car jitna bhi accelerate kare, speed limit (maxBackoffMs) se aage kabhi nahi ja sakti, chahe uska engine (attempt count) kitna bhi powerful ho.
how_it_works: Pure function: Math.min(maxMs, initialMs * Math.pow(2, attempt - 1)). No internal state, no side effects -- purely derived from the attempt count and the two configured bounds.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka top-level backoffMs function; iska caller dispatchChannel ke failure branch mein.
advantages: Pure function, trivially unit-testable without any scheduler state
Cap prevents unbounded growth -- predictable worst-case delay
disadvantages: No jitter -- many channels failing at the same moment will all retry at exactly the same computed delay (see SOC-124)
Exponential growth with no cap would otherwise explode fast; relying on a hardcoded cap is simple but not configurable per-failure-type
common_mistakes: Off-by-one: using attempt instead of attempt-1 in the exponent, which would double the very first backoff unexpectedly
Applying the cap only at the end of accumulated delay instead of per-call, which this implementation avoids by capping every single computation
follow_up_questions: What would backoffMs(1, 1000, 1000) return, and why does that make sense given the formula?
How would you verify, with a test, that the cap is actually applied and not just that backoff grows?

question: How exactly is editPost's 'zero attempts on every non-canceled channel' rule implemented?
answer_hinglish:
`editPost` ek for-loop chalata hai `Object.values(record.deliveries)` par, VALIDATION phase ke start mein (content/scheduledAt validate hone se pehle bhi) -- `for (const delivery of Object.values(record.deliveries)) { if (delivery.status === "canceled") continue; if (delivery.attempts > 0) throw POST_ALREADY_DISPATCHED; }`.

Loop ka logic exactly do lines mein hai: pehla check -- `status === 'canceled'` ho toh `continue` (skip, is delivery ko bilkul ignore karo, chahe uske attempts kuch bhi ho). Doosra check -- agar skip nahi hua, toh `attempts > 0` ho toh THROW, immediately, poore method se bahar.

Yeh order important hai: canceled check PEHLE hota hai, isliye ek canceled channel jiska `attempts` already `> 0` hai (mid-retry cancel ka scenario) us throw ko kabhi nahi hit karta -- woh `continue` se hi nikal jaata hai. Agar order reverse hota (attempts check pehle), toh ek canceled-but-previously-attempted channel bhi galat se block kar deta edit ko.

Loop poore `record.deliveries` par chalta hai, sirf first failing delivery par throw hota hai -- matlab agar MULTIPLE channels attempted hain, error message sirf ek channel ka naam carry karega (jo bhi Object.values() order mein pehle aaya), baaki check hi nahi hote kyunki throw method ko exit kar deta hai.
why_needed: Interviewer exact loop structure aur early-exit behavior check karna chahta hai -- yeh common interview follow-up hai jab candidate kahta hai 'editPost checks attempts > 0' bina yeh explain kiye ki canceled channels kaise skip hote hain.
real_world_analogy: Ek teacher class attendance check kar rahi hai 'sabne homework kiya ya nahi' -- jo student already absent mark hua (canceled) usse homework ka sawal hi nahi poochha jaata, baaki sab se poochha jaata hai, aur pehla jo 'nahi kiya' bole usi par teacher ruk jaati hai.
how_it_works: for-loop over Object.values(deliveries): canceled -> continue (never checked for attempts); else attempts > 0 -> throw POST_ALREADY_DISPATCHED immediately, short-circuiting the rest of the loop.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka editPost method, specifically the validation for-loop before content/scheduledAt are touched; test/cancel-edit.test.ts ka 'allows editing a post whose only channel was canceled AFTER an attempt'.
advantages: Two simple sequential checks, easy to read and reason about
Canceled-skip ordered first means a mid-retry-then-canceled channel never blocks the edit, matching the design intent
disadvantages: Error message only names the FIRST offending channel found via Object.values() iteration order, not every blocking channel

Object key iteration order (insertion order for string keys) is relied upon implicitly, though it does not affect correctness here since the loop checks ALL deliveries regardless of order until it throws
common_mistakes: Swapping the order of the two checks, which would incorrectly block edits around a mid-retry-then-canceled channel
Checking attempts > 0 across only non-canceled count aggregated, instead of per-delivery with per-delivery skip
follow_up_questions: What test would specifically catch the two checks being swapped (the exact mutation E3 found)?
If you wanted the error to list every blocking channel instead of just the first, how would you change this loop?

question: How does the idempotency fingerprint comparison work -- why is it order-independent across channels but not across content or scheduledAt?
answer_hinglish:
`fingerprintOf(content, channels, scheduledAt)` function hai: `return JSON.stringify({ content, channels: [...new Set(channels)].sort(), scheduledAt })`. Teen cheezein is object mein hain -- content (string, as-is), channels (TRANSFORMED), scheduledAt (number, as-is).

Channels transformation do steps mein hoti hai: `new Set(channels)` duplicates remove karta hai (though validation already duplicates reject karti hai, toh yeh practically redundant hai par safe hai), phir `[...set].sort()` ALPHABETICALLY sort karta hai array ko. Isliye `["twitter", "linkedin"]` aur `["linkedin", "twitter"]` dono SAME sorted array `["linkedin", "twitter"]` banate hain -- yehi wajah hai ki channel ORDER fingerprint ko affect nahi karta, bas SET of channels matter karta hai.

Content aur scheduledAt ko koi transformation nahi milta -- woh EXACT value honi chahiye match karne ke liye. Agar content ek character bhi different hai, `JSON.stringify` ka output different hoga, fingerprint mismatch hoga.

Comparison khud `schedulePost` mein hota hai: naya request ka fingerprint compute karo (`fingerprintOf` call karke SHAPE-validated content/channels/scheduledAt ke saath, chahe woh replay ho ya nahi), aur `existing.fingerprint` (jo ORIGINAL schedule time par stored hua tha) se STRING EQUALITY (`!==`) compare karo. Mismatch par `IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT`, match par original post return.
why_needed: Interviewer exact implementation detail (Set + sort + JSON.stringify) poochhta hai, yeh dekhne ke liye ki candidate 'order-independent comparison' ka ACTUAL mechanism samajhta hai, sirf result nahi.
real_world_analogy: Do grocery lists match karna chahiye content ke hisaab se, order ke hisaab se nahi -- 'milk, bread, eggs' aur 'eggs, milk, bread' SAME shopping trip hai, par 'milk, bread, eggs' aur 'milk, bread, cheese' DIFFERENT hai, chahe order kuch bhi ho.
how_it_works: fingerprintOf: JSON.stringify({ content, channels: [...new Set(channels)].sort(), scheduledAt }). Deduplicated+sorted channels make the fingerprint order-independent across channels; content and scheduledAt participate as exact values.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka top-level fingerprintOf function; schedulePost ke dono paths (replay check aur fresh record creation) mein isi function ka use.
advantages: Channel-order-independence matches the user-facing promise exactly (README: 'the same set of channels, order does not matter')
JSON.stringify gives a simple, deterministic string key without hashing
disadvantages: JSON.stringify-based fingerprints grow with content size -- fine for this project's in-memory scale, less ideal for a huge content field at real scale
Deduplication via Set is dead code in practice since requireChannelsShape already rejects duplicate channels before fingerprintOf is reached on the fresh-schedule path
common_mistakes: Comparing channels arrays directly without sorting, which would treat a reordered-but-identical channel list as a conflict
Forgetting that content and scheduledAt are NOT normalized -- they must match exactly, unlike channels
follow_up_questions: Why is the Set wrapper still useful even though schedulePost's own validation already rejects duplicate channels?
What would change in fingerprintOf if content needed to be compared case-insensitively?

question: Why is dispatchChannel's dispatching.delete(key) inside a finally block, and what breaks if it weren't?
answer_hinglish:
`dispatchChannel` ka poora body ek `try { ... } finally { this.dispatching.delete(key); }` structure mein hai. `finally` block GUARANTEE karta hai ki `delete(key)` chalega -- chahe `try` block normally complete ho (success ya failed-but-handled provider result), ya chahe andar kahin UNEXPECTED throw ho jaaye jo already catch nahi hua.

Note karo: `provider.send()` ka throw already andar ek NESTED try/catch se handled hota hai (treated as a failed attempt, 'result' bana diya jaata hai) -- isliye woh normally `finally` tak pahunchne se pehle hi handle ho jaata hai. Par `finally` ek EXTRA safety net hai agar KISI aur reason se (jaise `this.clock.now()` throw kare, ya koi future code change jo bina socha try block mein throw kare) method genuinely crash kare -- tab bhi `dispatching` Set se key hatana zaroori hai.

Agar `finally` nahi hota aur sirf `try` ke END mein `delete(key)` likha hota, toh ek UNEXPECTED throw (jo nested catch na pakde) us delete line ko kabhi reach nahi karne deta -- `key` PERMANENTLY `dispatching` Set mein reh jaata. Iska result: woh exact channel `tick()`'s scan mein HAMESHA exclude ho jaata (`!this.dispatching.has(key)` false ho jaata), aur `cancelChannel`/`cancelPost` bhi HAMESHA `DISPATCH_IN_PROGRESS` throw karte us channel ke liye -- ek PERMANENTLY stuck channel, kabhi dispatch nahi, kabhi cancel nahi.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate try/finally ka EXACT purpose samajhta hai is context mein -- resource cleanup guarantee, specifically jab exception paths involved hain.
real_world_analogy: Ek library book checkout system jahan 'book is checked out' flag HAMESHA hatana hai jab return process khatam ho, chahe return process EXACTLY kaise khatam ho (normally ya kisi error ke saath) -- warna book PERMANENTLY 'checked out' dikhti rahegi, koi aur kabhi issue nahi kar sakega.
how_it_works: try { attempts++; await provider.send() wrapped in its own try/catch; update status/backoff } finally { dispatching.delete(key) }. The finally runs on every exit path from the try block, normal or exceptional.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka dispatchChannel private method -- the outer try/finally wrapping the whole dispatch logic.
advantages: Guarantees the dispatching Set never leaks a stuck key, even under an unanticipated error
Separates 'normal failure handling' (the nested try/catch around provider.send()) from 'guaranteed cleanup' (the outer finally) -- two different concerns, two different mechanisms
disadvantages: A genuinely stuck key (from a bug elsewhere) would still be undetectable from the outside since dispatching is private
The safety net only matters for truly unexpected errors -- the expected failure path (provider throws) is already handled before it would ever reach this concern
common_mistakes: Putting dispatching.delete(key) only at the end of the try block instead of in finally, assuming the nested catch covers every possible failure
Assuming finally changes the method's return value or re-throws -- it only runs cleanup, the original throw (if any) still propagates after finally completes
follow_up_questions: What test would prove this finally actually matters, versus just appearing defensive?
If dispatchChannel's provider.send() call were NOT wrapped in its own try/catch, would the outer finally still be enough to keep the system correct?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Outer finally ek defensive guarantee hai jiska cost bahut kam hai (ek extra delete call) par value sirf UNEXPECTED errors ke against hai -- is project ka actual, expected failure path (provider throws/rejects) already andar handle hota hai, isliye yeh finally zyada ek 'belt and suspenders' safety net hai, primary mechanism nahi.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar koi future code change (jaise ek naya side-effect provider.send() se PEHLE) genuinely throw kare bina try/catch ke andar hue, finally nahi hone ki surat mein woh specific channel PERMANENTLY stuck ho jaata -- na dispatch, na cancel, forever.
advanced.alternatives: Ek explicit cleanup helper function jo HAR exit point par manually call ho (zyada error-prone, duplicate code); ya ek wrapper/decorator jo automatically claim-and-release pattern enforce kare (zyada abstraction, is scale ke liye overkill).
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Yeh guarantee scale-independent hai -- ek single stuck key bhi bahut problematic hai chahe 10 channels hon ya 10 lakh, kyunki woh specific channel kabhi progress nahi karega. Scale badhne se is guarantee ki ZAROORAT nahi badhti, par ek stuck key ko MANUALLY detect karna bahut harder ho jaata hai zyada channels ke beech.
advanced.production_improvements: Dispatching Set ki size/age ko monitoring mein expose karna (abhi private hai) taaki ek stuck key production mein jaldi detectable ho, is finally guarantee ke bawajood bhi (defense in depth).

question: There's a window between tick()'s scan phase and its claim phase where both run synchronously -- how does requireNotDispatching's check interact with that timing, and is there still a race?
answer_hinglish:
`tick()` ka scan loop aur claim loop DONO fully synchronous hain, EK HI function call ke andar, koi await beech mein nahi -- isliye JavaScript ke run-to-completion model ki wajah se, JAB TAK `tick()` ka pehla `await` (jo `Promise.all` ke andar hai) nahi lagta, koi doosra code (koi `cancelChannel` call, koi doosra `tick()` call) beech mein interleave NAHI ho sakta. Matlab scan aur claim ke beech mein genuinely koi race window hai hi nahi JS single-threaded event loop mein -- yeh wahi guarantee hai jo SOC-106 mein schedulePost ke liye discuss hui.

`requireNotDispatching` (jo `cancelChannel`/`cancelPost` use karte hain) is `dispatching` Set ko check karta hai -- `if (this.dispatching.has(key)) throw DISPATCH_IN_PROGRESS`. Yeh method sirf TAB meaningful hai jab `cancelChannel` ek `tick()` call ke AWAIT ke dauraan chale -- us waqt `dispatching` Set mein key already add ho chuki hai (claim phase complete ho chuka tha before the await), isliye `requireNotDispatching` correctly DISPATCH_IN_PROGRESS throw karega.

Actual race jo EXIST karti hai: ek `tick()` call `await Promise.all(...)` par ruka hai, us waqt EK channel ka `dispatchChannel` andar `await provider.send()` par ruka hai -- ISI waqt agar `cancelChannel` call ho, `requireNotDispatching` use detect kar leta hai kyunki key already `dispatching` mein hai. Yeh exact scenario `test/dispatch-guard.test.ts` mein manually-resolved provider se test kiya gaya hai -- har DOOSRA provider is project mein turant resolve hota hai, isliye koi aur test file yeh genuinely exercise hi nahi karta.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate synchronous-vs-asynchronous race windows ka FARAK samajhta hai -- kahan JS ki single-threaded guarantee kaafi hai, aur kahan ek explicit guard (dispatching Set) genuinely zaroori hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek clerk jo pehle SAARI files ek saath uthata hai apne desk par (scan+claim, ek breath mein), phir unhe EK-EK karke process karna shuru karta hai, har file ke beech mein ek break leta hai (await) -- koi doosra clerk usi file ko tabhi touch kar sakta hai jab woh already uthayi hui ho AUR ek break ke dauraan ho.
how_it_works: Scan+claim is one synchronous block, no race possible there. The real race window is during dispatchChannel's single await (provider.send()) -- that's exactly where requireNotDispatching's check matters, because the dispatching Set was already populated before that await started.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka tick() (synchronous scan+claim) aur requireNotDispatching; test/dispatch-guard.test.ts jo is exact window ko deferred provider se exercise karta hai.
advantages: No race exists within the synchronous scan+claim block -- no extra guard needed there
The dispatching guard precisely targets the ONE real race window (the await inside dispatchChannel), rather than over-guarding everything
disadvantages: Understanding WHY there's no race in the scan+claim phase requires knowing JS's run-to-completion model -- not obvious to someone assuming true parallelism
A caller unfamiliar with this project could add an await somewhere in the scan/claim phase without realizing it reintroduces a genuine race
common_mistakes: Assuming a race exists between scan and claim just because they are two separate loops -- they are still one synchronous call
Assuming requireNotDispatching protects against every possible race, when it specifically targets the dispatchChannel await window
follow_up_questions: If an await were introduced between the scan loop and the claim loop inside tick(), what new race would open up?
Why does test/dispatch-guard.test.ts need a manually-resolved provider instead of using any of the existing fake providers?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Relying on JS's synchronous run-to-completion for the scan+claim phase avoids an explicit lock there, keeping tick() simple -- but this is implicit, undocumented-at-the-type-level safety that depends on no future await being introduced mid-phase.
advanced.failure_scenarios: If a future refactor split the scan and claim loops across an await (e.g. an async filter), two overlapping tick() calls could both scan before either claims, double-dispatching the same channel -- exactly the bug the dispatching Set exists to prevent, reintroduced by breaking the synchronous assumption.
advanced.alternatives: Combine scan and claim into a single pass (filter-and-add in one loop) to make the synchronous requirement more visually obvious in the code, even though behaviorally it is already equivalent.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: This reasoning is scale-independent within one process -- it depends on the event loop model, not on data volume. It breaks down entirely, regardless of scale, the moment multiple processes are involved (see SOC-110), since JS's single-threaded guarantee only holds within one process.
advanced.production_improvements: Add a comment or a lint rule flagging any new await introduced between the scan and claim loops in tick(), since that boundary is where this project's race-safety assumption lives.

question: In schedulePost, why does the idempotency replay check run AFTER the clientRequestId shape check but BEFORE the channel/content/scheduledAt semantic checks?
answer_hinglish:
`schedulePost` ka validation order EXACTLY teen tiers mein hai, aur order DELIBERATE hai. Tier 1: `requireClientRequestId` -- yeh ALWAYS chalta hai, replay ho ya na ho, kyunki ek malformed `clientRequestId` ek 400-style error hai REGARDLESS of whether it is a replay (tum ek invalid key se kabhi lookup bhi nahi kar sakte).

Tier 2: idempotency map lookup -- `this.idempotency.get(clientRequestId)`. Agar key MILTI hai, yeh REPLAY hai -- aur ek replay apne FINGERPRINT se match karega, original request ke deeper semantic checks (unknown channel, past scheduledAt) ko RE-RUN nahi karega. Yeh important hai: agar original request VALID tha jab accept hua, ek replay (SAME exact data ke saath) usko dobara reject NAHI karna chahiye sirf isliye ki duniya mein kuch badal gaya (jaise clock aage badh gaya aur `scheduledAt` ab 'past' lag raha hai).

Tier 3 (sirf agar replay NAHI hai): `requireContent`, `requireValidChannels` (jo UNKNOWN_CHANNEL check karta hai), `requireFutureScheduledAt`. Yeh sab sirf EK FRESH request ke liye chalte hain.

Note karo: fingerprint COMPUTE karne ke liye SHAPE checks (`requireContent`, `requireChannelsShape`, `requireScheduledAtShape`) replay path mein BHI chalte hain -- kyunki fingerprint banane ke liye content/channels/scheduledAt ka VALID shape chahiye hi hota hai, par UNKNOWN_CHANNEL jaisa SEMANTIC check replay path mein skip ho jaata hai.
why_needed: Interviewer exact validation-tier ordering poochhta hai -- yeh dikhata hai ki candidate samajhta hai 'a replay answers from the stored result, it does not re-validate the original request' ka implementation-level implication.
real_world_analogy: Ek courier jo ek PEHLE SE DELIVERED package ka tracking number dobara scan kare -- woh usse 'already delivered, here's your receipt' bolega, dobara address verify nahi karega ya dobara check nahi karega ki address abhi bhi valid hai ya nahi.
how_it_works: requireClientRequestId (always) -> idempotency.get() lookup -> if found: compute fingerprint via SHAPE-only checks, compare, return existing or throw IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT -> if not found: full semantic validation (content, channels incl. UNKNOWN_CHANNEL, future scheduledAt) -> build and store.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka schedulePost method -- the comment directly above it ('The idempotency check itself runs AFTER the cheap shape checks... BEFORE the deeper semantic checks') and the requireChannelsShape vs requireValidChannels distinction.
advantages: A replay of an originally-valid request never fails later due to the world changing (e.g. clock advancing past the original scheduledAt)
clientRequestId shape is validated unconditionally -- you can't even attempt a lookup with a malformed key
disadvantages: requireChannelsShape and requireValidChannels being two separate methods (shape-only vs shape+semantic) adds a layer of indirection a reader has to notice
A replay with a channel that's since had its provider REMOVED from the providers map would still succeed, since UNKNOWN_CHANNEL is never re-checked
common_mistakes: Running requireValidChannels (with the UNKNOWN_CHANNEL check) on the replay path, which would incorrectly fail a replay if a provider was removed after the original schedule succeeded
Skipping requireClientRequestId's shape check before the idempotency lookup, risking a lookup with garbage input
follow_up_questions: What would happen on a replay if a provider for one of the original channels were removed from the providers map in between?
Why is it safe for the replay path to skip the SCHEDULED_AT_IN_PAST check specifically?

question: Walk through the stage 2 change that added a retryable-vs-permanent failure distinction -- exactly what changed in types.ts, providers.ts and dispatchChannel, and how was it proven not to break any existing dead-letter test?
answer_hinglish:
Change teen jagah hai, aur teeno chhote hain.

(1) src/types.ts: ProviderResult ka failed variant ab `{ status: "failed"; reason: string; retryable?: boolean }` hai -- optional, absent matlab retryable.

(2) src/scheduler.ts dispatchChannel ka failure branch: `lastError` pehle jaisa set hota hai, phir `const permanent = result.retryable === false; if (permanent || delivery.attempts >= delivery.maxAttempts) dead_letter; else backoff`. backoffMs formula untouched hai -- permanent failure usse skip karti hai, badalti nahi. `attempts` pehle jaisa await se pehle increment hota hai, permanent ke liye bhi.

(3) src/providers.ts: AlwaysFailsProvider ko doosra constructor param mila, `retryable = true` -- naya class nahi. send() `retryable` key sirf false hone par emit karta hai, isliye `new AlwaysFailsProvider("nope")` ka result abhi bhi exactly `{ status: "failed", reason: "nope" }` hai aur purana `toEqual` assertion bina change pass hota hai. FlakyProvider untouched -- woh temporary outage model karta hai, jo inherently retryable hai.

Proof: stage 1 ke 84 tests unmodified chale aur pass hue (ab total 90). Naye: 4 tick tests (attempt 1 par dead-letter, succeeding sibling, flaky sibling, retryable-then-permanent sequence), 2 provider-shape tests, aur invariant test mein ek chautha permanent provider. 13 mutation checks, sab caught; R9 (default false kar do) ne 12 stage-1 tests tode -- matlab purane tests sach mein 'default retryable' pin karte hain, coincidence se pass nahi ho rahe.
why_needed: Advanced interviewer 'design it' se aage jaa kar dekhna chahta hai ki tum ek backward-compatible change ko file-by-file explain kar sakte ho, aur 'kuch nahi toota' ko evidence se prove kar sakte ho, sirf claim se nahi.
real_world_analogy: Ek courier company ne 'address exist nahi karta' ka naya return code add kiya. Purane scanners jo yeh code bhejte hi nahi, unke packages pehle jaise 3 baar try hote hain. Naye scanners yeh code bhejte hain toh package pehli baar mein hi return ho jaata hai -- aur kisi purane scanner ko update nahi karna pada.
how_it_works: attempts += 1 (sync, await se pehle) -> await provider.send() (throw hua toh catch ek failed result banata hai bina retryable ke) -> sent? providerId/sentAt record : { lastError = reason; permanent = retryable === false; permanent || attempts >= maxAttempts ? dead_letter : nextAttemptAt = now + backoffMs(attempts) } -> finally dispatching.delete(key).
in_this_project: test/tick.test.ts ka describe 'permanent failures (retryable: false)': 'dead-letters on the very first attempt, skipping the retry schedule entirely' (maxAttempts 5, attempts 1), 'does not affect a sibling channel that succeeds', 'does not affect a sibling channel that is still retrying via a flaky provider', 'attempt 1 retryable, attempt 2 permanent: dead-letters after exactly 2 attempts, not maxAttempts'. test/providers.test.ts: 'defaults to retryable: true, and does not put a retryable field on the result at all' aur 'can be constructed to fail permanently (retryable: false)'. README.md 'Mutation checks' ka stage 2 table (R1-R13).
advantages: Three small, local edits; no stage 1 test or call site had to change
A permanent failure dead-letters on the attempt it happens, so the dead_letter signal is immediate and the provider is not called again
Sibling channels stay fully independent, proven by two dedicated tests
disadvantages: The dead_letter record does not store WHY it dead-lettered; you infer it from lastError and attempts < maxAttempts
Correctness depends on providers classifying their errors correctly; the scheduler cannot verify it
common_mistakes: Writing `!result.retryable` instead of `=== false`, which turns every old failure permanent (the R4-style break)
Dropping the `attempts >= maxAttempts` half of the OR, so retryable failures never dead-letter (R5/R6)
Decrementing attempts for a permanent failure to 'not count' it (R13) -- the provider really was called
Emitting `retryable: true` explicitly from AlwaysFailsProvider, which breaks the existing toEqual shape test
follow_up_questions: Why is the permanent variant a constructor option and not a new provider class?
How did the invariant test's dead_letter rule have to change?
What would it have meant if mutation R9 had survived?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Permanent ko dead-letter condition mein ek OR clause banana sabse kam invasive raasta tha -- na naya status, na ChannelDelivery par naya field, na backoff formula mein change. Trade: dead_letter ab do alag causes represent karta hai bina unhe distinguish kiye.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Mixed sequence: attempt 1 retryable fail -> pending + backoff; attempt 2 permanent -> dead_letter at attempts 2, maxAttempts 5 nahi (tested). Uske baad editPost POST_ALREADY_DISPATCHED dega (attempts > 0) aur cancelChannel CHANNEL_NOT_PENDING (terminal hai). Ek provider jo galti se transient error ko retryable: false bol de, recoverable post ko early dead-letter karega -- scheduler isse detect nahi kar sakta.
advanced.alternatives: Ek alag 'failed_permanent' status (rejected: one status enum rule); ek separate AlwaysFailsPermanentlyProvider class (rejected: FlakyProvider ke failCount jaisa constructor knob hi kaafi hai); retryable ko required banana (rejected: stage 1 providers ke liye breaking change).
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Logic per dispatch O(1) hai, scale par koi naya cost nahi. Bada asar operational hai: permanent failures turant terminal ho jaati hain, toh pending backlog jo tick() har call par scan karta hai, chhota rehta hai.
advanced.production_improvements: ChannelDelivery par ek deadLetterCause ('permanent' | 'exhausted') field, metrics mein dono alag count, aur real providers ke error-code -> retryable mapping ko contract tests se pin karna. Yeh is project mein abhi built nahi hai.

question: Design per-channel content length limits so that schedulePost and editPost both enforce them consistently.
answer_hinglish:
Core challenge: content EK field hai poore post par, par limit CHANNEL-specific honi chahiye. Design: ek `CHANNEL_LIMITS: Record<string, number>` config object (ya constructor option, `SchedulerOptions.channelContentLimits?: Record<string, number>`), default fallback `MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH` agar kisi channel ka specific limit na diya gaya ho.

`requireContent` ko extend karna hoga ek naya parameter lena: `requireContent(content: unknown, channels: readonly string[])`. Andar, HAR targeted channel ke limit nikalo aur SABSE CHHOTA lo: `const limit = Math.min(...channels.map(c => this.channelContentLimits[c] ?? MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH))`, phir `content.length > limit` check karo.

Sabse tricky part: `schedulePost` mein, `requireContent` ABHI `requireValidChannels` se PEHLE call hota hai (order dekho current code mein) -- naya design mein content check channel-dependent hai, isliye ORDER FLIP karna padega: pehle channels validate/shape karo, PHIR content ko unhi channels ke against check karo. `editPost` mein bhi same tarika -- agar sirf content badal raha hai, EXISTING `record.channels` use karo limit compute karne ke liye; agar koi future design channel-list-edit bhi allow kare (abhi nahi hai, SOC-127 dekho), tab naye channels use honge.

Edge case: schedulePost's IDEMPOTENCY REPLAY path bhi `requireContent` call karta hai fingerprint banane ke liye (shape-only abhi) -- yeh SHAPE check hai, channel-specific length check NAHI honi chahiye replay path par (SOC-121 ka reasoning: replay re-validate nahi karta).
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate ek seemingly-simple feature request (per-channel limits) ke andar hidden complexity (ordering dependency, replay-path interaction) dhoondh sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek speech jo tumhe alag venues mein deni hai, jahan har venue ka apna time-limit hai -- tumhe apni speech ko venue list dekhne ke BAAD measure karna padega (channels check pehle), content measure karne se pehle, warna tumhe pata hi nahi chalega kis limit ke against check karna hai.
how_it_works: Validate channels first (to know which limits apply), then validate content against the MINIMUM limit among this post's target channels. Idempotency replay path keeps using shape-only content validation, not the new per-channel length check.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka requireContent, requireValidChannels, schedulePost (current call order), editPost.
advantages: Reuses the existing requireContent as a base layer, only adding a channel-aware check on top
A post is guaranteed postable on every one of its target channels at schedule time, not discovered as a per-channel failure at dispatch time
disadvantages: Forces content down to the tightest channel's limit even when other channels could accept more -- no per-channel content variation
Requires reordering validation in schedulePost (channels before content), a non-trivial refactor given how idempotency replay currently calls requireContent early for fingerprinting
common_mistakes: Applying the new per-channel check to the idempotency replay's fingerprint-shape validation, which should remain shape-only
Forgetting editPost needs the same per-channel check when content is being changed, using the post's EXISTING channel list
follow_up_questions: How would this design change if a post could target channels with wildly different limits (e.g. 50 vs 3000 characters) and the caller wanted per-channel content instead of one shared field?
What happens to this check if editPost someday allows adding a new channel to an existing post?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Keeping content as ONE field and enforcing the tightest limit is the simplest extension of the current design, but it fundamentally caps what a post can say to its most permissive channels, trading flexibility for simplicity -- a per-channel content model would remove that cap but is a bigger redesign (touching ScheduledPost's shape itself).
advanced.failure_scenarios: A caller targeting Twitter and LinkedIn together would have their LinkedIn post artificially truncated to Twitter's limit at validation time, which could confuse a caller who expected LinkedIn to get the full-length version -- a documentation/error-message clarity issue more than a correctness bug.
advanced.alternatives: Add an OPTIONAL per-channel content override map alongside the base content field (channels without an override use the base content, checked against their own limit); this is a bigger type change but solves the flexibility problem directly.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: This validation cost is O(channels per post), negligible at any scale this project targets. The real scaling question is whether per-channel content overrides (the alternative above) become necessary as the number of distinct channel types grows.
advanced.production_improvements: Ship the tightest-limit version first (smallest change, matches real Twitter/LinkedIn-style limits), then evaluate whether real usage needs per-channel content overrides before building that bigger feature.

question: Design a real job queue with leases for multiple concurrent dispatch workers, reusing project 21's design, without a full rewrite of SocialScheduler.
answer_hinglish:
Project 21's `JobQueue` interface (`claim`, `owns`, `complete`, `reschedule`) already generic hai -- is project mein isko REUSE karne ka sabse clean tarika yeh hai ki `tick()` ko redesign karo taaki woh due-channel SCAN khud na kare, balki `JobQueue.claim(now, max, leaseMs)` call kare jo already ready jobs return karta hai leaseToken ke saath.

Har 'job' ek `postId:channel` pair represent karega. `dispatchChannel`'s core logic (attempts++, provider.send(), status update) WAISA HI rehta hai -- bas ab yeh ek `ClaimedJob` leta hai jiske paas `leaseToken` hai, aur complete hone par `queue.owns(id, leaseToken, now)` check karta hai BEFORE committing the status change (taaki agar lease expire ho gaya ho AUR koi doosra worker ne already job reclaim kar liya ho, yeh worker apna STALE result commit na kare) -- yeh `complete()`/`reschedule()` calls ke through hota hai jo khud internally `owns` check karte hain.

`posts` Map ko bhi ek SHARED backend mein jaana hoga (abhi in-memory hai, per-instance) -- yeh sabse bada structural change hai, kyunki `SocialScheduler` abhi assume karta hai ki `this.posts` sirf usi process mein accessible hai. Minimal viable version: `posts`/`idempotency` ko ABHI bhi in-memory rakho EK SHARED process mein (jaise ek single scheduler-coordinator service), par MULTIPLE WORKER processes sirf `JobQueue` ke through jobs claim karen aur dispatch karen, result wapas coordinator ko REPORT karen (RPC/message queue se) jo `posts` Map update kare. Yeh poora redesign nahi hai `dispatchChannel`'s core logic ka -- sirf `tick()`'s due-detection aur claim mechanism badalta hai, aur commit-reporting ek naya step hai.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate ek EXISTING reusable component (project 21's JobQueue) ko is project ke context mein wire kar sakta hai, bina core dispatch logic (dispatchChannel) ko rewrite kiye.
real_world_analogy: Ek call center jo apne existing ticket-claiming system (jo already kisi doosre department mein kaam kar raha hai) ko reuse kare, instead of naya system banaye -- agents ka actual call-handling kaam (dispatchChannel jaisa) same rehta hai, sirf 'kaunsa agent kaunsa ticket uthaye' logic badalta hai.
how_it_works: tick() delegates due-detection+claiming to JobQueue.claim(). dispatchChannel's core logic stays the same but checks queue.owns() before committing, and reports completion/reschedule via queue.complete()/reschedule(). posts/idempotency state needs a shared backend for true multi-process workers.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka current tick()/dispatchChannel (in-process scan+dispatching Set); project 21's src/queue.ts (JobQueue interface, InMemoryJobQueue) and src/worker.ts as the reusable reference.
advantages: Reuses a proven, already-tested design (project 21's JobQueue) instead of inventing a new concurrency primitive
dispatchChannel's core send/retry/backoff logic is preserved almost unchanged -- the change is concentrated in how work is claimed and committed
disadvantages: posts/idempotency state still needs a real shared backend for true multi-process correctness -- the job queue alone does not solve that
Introduces a new failure mode: a worker's result arriving after its lease expired must be discarded, which needs careful handling to avoid silently losing a successful send
common_mistakes: Wiring in the JobQueue for claiming jobs but forgetting the owns() check before committing a result, risking a stale worker overwriting a reclaimed job's state
Assuming the JobQueue alone makes posts/idempotency safe across processes -- they are separate concerns
follow_up_questions: What happens to a channel's attempts count if two workers both claim it due to a lease racing right at expiry?
How would you choose leaseMs relative to how long a real provider.send() call is expected to take?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Reusing project 21's JobQueue interface wholesale keeps this project's own code additions small, but couples its concurrency model to a design built for a DIFFERENT project's needs -- any JobQueue limitation (e.g. O(n) claim scan in InMemoryJobQueue) is inherited as-is unless also addressed.
advanced.failure_scenarios: A worker that claims a job, starts dispatchChannel's provider.send(), then stalls past leaseMs (e.g. a slow network call) will have its job reclaimed by another worker mid-flight -- when the first worker's send() eventually resolves, owns() correctly tells it to discard the result, but the ACTUAL provider call may have already succeeded, meaning the channel could be double-sent to the real platform unless the provider itself is idempotent.
advanced.alternatives: A fully external message queue (SQS/RabbitMQ) instead of a custom lease-based InMemoryJobQueue, trading custom code for operational infrastructure; or a database-backed queue (Postgres SKIP LOCKED, as InMemoryJobQueue's own comment references) for both leasing and durable state in one place.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At 10x worker count, the shared JobQueue backend becomes the new bottleneck (claim() contention) rather than any single worker's CPU. At 100x, InMemoryJobQueue's O(n) claim scan (same shape as this project's tick() scan, see SOC-114) would need its own indexing fix to keep up.
advanced.production_improvements: Move the JobQueue itself to a durable, indexed backend (Postgres with SKIP LOCKED, or a managed queue service). Make real providers idempotent (so a double-send from a lease race is harmless) wherever the underlying platform API allows it (e.g. an idempotency key the platform itself honors).

question: Design idempotency key expiry with an LRU bound, similar to what project 21 stage 2 would need, for this project's idempotency Map.
answer_hinglish:
Abhi `this.idempotency = new Map<string, string>()` kabhi shrink nahi hota -- har naya `clientRequestId` permanently is Map mein reh jaata hai, memory traffic ke saath grow karti hai, README mein yeh explicitly 'Known and NOT handled' mein documented hai.

LRU (Least Recently Used) bound design: ek MAX_IDEMPOTENCY_KEYS limit set karo (jaise 100,000). Jab limit hit ho, SABSE PURANA (least-recently-accessed) key evict karo naya add karne se pehle. JavaScript ka `Map` already INSERTION ORDER maintain karta hai iteration ke liye -- par 'recently used' track karne ke liye, HAR access (lookup, not just insert) par key ko RE-INSERT karna padega (delete + set) taaki woh Map ke END mein chali jaaye 'most recently used' ban kar.

Actual integration point: `schedulePost`'s idempotency lookup (`this.idempotency.get(clientRequestId)`) ko wrap karna hoga ek helper mein jo access par bhi re-insert kare. Naya key add karte waqt (`this.idempotency.set(...)` call se pehle), size check karo -- agar `size >= MAX_IDEMPOTENCY_KEYS`, Map ka FIRST key (`this.idempotency.keys().next().value`, jo least-recently-used hai insertion-order ki wajah se) delete karo.

CRITICAL risk: agar ek key EVICT ho jaaye jiska POST abhi bhi `posts` Map mein exist karta hai, ek REPLAY us clientRequestId ke saath ab 'naya' treat hoga (idempotency check miss ho jaayega) aur ek DUPLICATE post ban jaayega -- same clientRequestId, do alag posts. Yeh ek genuine trade-off hai jo project 21 ka TTL+LRU design bhi accept karta hai: bahut purani, LIKELY-NEVER-REPLAYED requests ka dedupe guarantee kho jaata hai memory bound ke against.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate bounded-memory data structures (LRU) design kar sakta hai AUR is design ka real correctness trade-off (eviction = lost dedupe guarantee) explicitly articulate kar sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek fridge jisme limited space hai -- naya khaana rakhne ke liye sabse PURANA (jo sabse kam use hua) item hatana padta hai. Agar koi item hata diya aur woh asal mein kisi ko abhi bhi chahiye tha, woh dobara order karna padega -- bilkul naya samajh kar.
how_it_works: Map's insertion order is repurposed as LRU order: every get() re-inserts the accessed key (delete+set) to move it to the 'most recent' end. On a new set(), if size exceeds the bound, the first (oldest) key is evicted.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka idempotency Map (currently unbounded) inside SocialScheduler; schedulePost's get()/set() calls on it.
advantages: Memory stays bounded regardless of traffic volume, unlike the current unbounded Map
Reuses JavaScript's native Map insertion-order behavior -- no separate linked-list bookkeeping needed
disadvantages: An evicted key silently loses its dedupe guarantee -- a very late, legitimate replay becomes a duplicate post instead of IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT-or-replay
Every lookup now does an extra delete+set to maintain LRU order, a small but real cost on the hot schedulePost path
common_mistakes: Checking size and evicting BEFORE adding the new key instead of after, which can evict the just-inserted key if the check is off by one
Forgetting to re-insert on READ (not just on write), which would make this a simple FIFO bound instead of a true LRU
follow_up_questions: Why is a time-based TTL (expire after N hours) a different trade-off than a size-based LRU bound, and could you combine both?
What would you log or monitor to know how often legitimate replays are being lost to eviction in production?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: LRU bound trades perfect dedupe correctness for bounded memory -- this is the same trade-off project 21 stage 2 documents for its own idempotency keys. The alternative, a TTL-based expiry, trades a DIFFERENT axis (time since creation vs. recency of access), and the two can be combined (whichever fires first evicts).
advanced.failure_scenarios: A caller that retries a schedulePost call after an unusually long delay (e.g. a client that batches retries and replays after hours), on a system under heavy unrelated traffic, could have its key evicted in between -- the retry would then create a genuine duplicate post instead of returning the original.
advanced.alternatives: A TTL-only expiry (simpler, bounded by time not memory, but can still grow unbounded under high enough sustained traffic); a hybrid LRU+TTL (evict on whichever limit is hit first, matching project 21's actual design); or moving idempotency keys to an external store (Redis with native TTL) which handles both concerns outside the process's own memory.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At 10x traffic, a fixed-size LRU bound holds up fine -- it just evicts more aggressively, shortening the EFFECTIVE replay window. At 100x, if replay windows need to stay long (e.g. clients that can legitimately retry after hours), the bound would need to grow correspondingly, which reintroduces the original unbounded-memory problem unless paired with external storage.
advanced.production_improvements: Add the LRU bound as a quick, self-contained fix today. Separately, plan a migration to an external TTL-capable store (Redis) for idempotency keys once this moves to a real multi-instance deployment, matching project 21's eventual design.

question: Add jitter to the backoff delay to avoid a thundering herd of many channels retrying at the exact same moment. Where exactly does this go, and what must NOT change?
answer_hinglish:
Problem: `backoffMs(attempt, initialMs, maxMs) = min(maxMs, initialMs * 2^(attempt-1))` ek PURE, DETERMINISTIC function hai -- SAME attempt number, SAME initialMs/maxMs ke saath, HAMESHA EXACT SAME delay deta hai. Agar bahut saare channels EK SAME waqt par fail hon (jaise ek platform-wide outage), sab EXACTLY SAME `nextAttemptAt` par phir se due ho jaayenge -- ek 'thundering herd' jahan sab EK SAME tick() call mein ek saath retry karte hain, provider par ek bada spike daal dete hain exactly jab woh already struggling tha.

Jitter fix: backoff delay mein ek SMALL RANDOM component add karo. Standard pattern: 'full jitter' -- `actualDelay = random(0, computedBackoff)` -- ya 'equal jitter' -- `actualDelay = computedBackoff/2 + random(0, computedBackoff/2)`. Is project mein, change `dispatchChannel`'s failure branch mein jaayega, JAHAN `nextAttemptAt` compute hota hai: `delivery.nextAttemptAt = now + jitter(backoffMs(delivery.attempts, this.initialBackoffMs, this.maxBackoffMs))`.

CRITICAL constraint: `backoffMs` khud PURE rehna chahiye -- usko mutate nahi karna. Jitter EK ALAG function honi chahiye jo `backoffMs`'s output ko wrap kare, taaki EXISTING tests jo `backoffMs(attempt, ...)` ko DIRECTLY call karte hain (determinstic output expect karte hue) UNAFFECTED rahein. Ek TESTABILITY concern bhi hai: random jitter test karna mushkil hai bina ek injected random source ke -- is project mein `Clock` jaisa hi ek injectable `rng: () => number` parameter add karna chahiye, taaki tests deterministic seed de sakein (jaisa `test/invariants.test.ts` ka `prng(seed)` pattern already karta hai).
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate jitter ka PURPOSE (thundering herd avoid karna) samajhta hai, aur yeh bhi ki random behavior ko TESTABLE kaise banate hain (injected RNG, same pattern jaisa Clock injection).
real_world_analogy: Ek office mein sab employees ki lunch break EXACTLY 1:00 PM par ho toh cafeteria overload ho jaata hai -- agar har employee ka break time thoda RANDOM stagger kiya jaaye (1:00-1:15 ke beech), cafeteria load spread ho jaata hai bina kisi ek employee ke break time ko significantly change kiye.
how_it_works: jitter(baseMs, rng) returns a randomized delay derived from baseMs (e.g. full jitter: rng() * baseMs). dispatchChannel's nextAttemptAt computation wraps backoffMs's deterministic output with this jitter function, using an injected rng source for testability.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka backoffMs (stays pure) aur dispatchChannel's failure branch (where nextAttemptAt is set) -- the integration point for a new jitter wrapper.
advantages: Spreads retry load over time instead of all channels retrying in lockstep, reducing the spike a recovering provider sees
backoffMs stays pure and unchanged, so every existing deterministic backoff test keeps passing untouched
disadvantages: Makes nextAttemptAt non-deterministic, which complicates any test asserting an EXACT delay value (tests now must assert a RANGE)
Full jitter can occasionally produce a very short delay (close to 0), retrying almost immediately -- a deliberate trade for better spread, not a bug
common_mistakes: Adding randomness directly inside backoffMs instead of wrapping its output, breaking its purity and every existing test that expects a deterministic value
Using Math.random() directly instead of an injected rng, making the new behavior untestable with a fixed seed
follow_up_questions: Why is full jitter (0 to baseMs) sometimes preferred over equal jitter (baseMs/2 to baseMs), and what's the trade-off between them?
How would you write a test that proves jitter is applied without asserting an exact nextAttemptAt value?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Wrapping backoffMs's output (rather than modifying it) preserves a clean separation: backoffMs answers 'what is the nominal delay', jitter answers 'how do we spread load around that nominal delay' -- two composable, independently testable concerns instead of one tangled function.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Without jitter, a provider-wide outage affecting many channels at once (e.g. a platform-wide API degradation) causes every affected channel to retry in near-perfect lockstep at each backoff boundary, repeatedly hammering an already-struggling provider with synchronized bursts instead of a spread-out trickle.
advanced.alternatives: Equal jitter (less variance, still spreads load, retries never get TOO short); decorrelated jitter (AWS's recommended scheme, which also factors in the previous delay); or jittering only above a certain attempt count, keeping early retries deterministic and fast.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At 10x channels, jitter's benefit is modest since collisions are rarer. At 100x+ channels sharing one provider, jitter becomes essential -- without it, a provider recovering from an outage would face recurring synchronized retry storms at every backoff interval, potentially never fully recovering.
advanced.production_improvements: Ship full or equal jitter as the default. Expose the rng as an injectable constructor option (mirroring Clock) so tests stay deterministic. Monitor actual retry timing distribution in production to confirm the jitter is achieving real spread, not just theoretically.

question: Design support for editing a post's channel list itself (adding or removing a channel), which editPost currently does not support at all.
answer_hinglish:
Abhi `editPost` sirf `content`/`scheduledAt` accept karta hai -- README explicitly kehta hai 'Editing the channel list itself is not supported... to add or remove a channel, cancel that one channel (or the whole post) and schedule a new one.' Yeh workaround kaam karta hai par ek NAYA post id banata hai, jo caller-side tracking complicate karta hai (same logical 'campaign' ab do post ids mein split ho gaya).

Design for channel-list editing: `EditPostRequest` mein ek naya optional field, `addChannels?: string[]` aur `removeChannels?: string[]`. REMOVE ek channel ke liye, SIMPLEST approach: internally `cancelChannel`'s logic reuse karo (status pending hone chahiye, nahi toh error) -- removed channel `canceled` ban jaata hai, delete nahi hota (history preserve karne ke liye, same jaise cancel karta hai).

ADD ek channel ke liye, zyada tricky hai: naya channel validate karna hoga (`UNKNOWN_CHANNEL` same jaisa schedulePost mein), aur naya `ChannelDelivery` banana hoga `status: pending, attempts: 0, nextAttemptAt: record.scheduledAt`. Par IMPORTANT edge case: agar edit mein `scheduledAt` BHI badal raha hai saath mein, naya channel ka `nextAttemptAt` NAYE `scheduledAt` ko use karega (jaisa existing pending channels already karte hain existing editPost code mein).

Sabse bada DESIGN QUESTION: kya naya channel add karna EXISTING attempts>0 restriction ke against bhi check hona chahiye? Reasoning: ek naya channel ne kabhi KUCH attempt nahi kiya -- isliye ADD karna hamesha safe hona CHAHIYE, chahe doosre channels already attempted hon (jo already EDIT content ko block karta hai, par add-only operation content nahi badal raha). Yeh matlab `addChannels` ek SEPARATE, LESS RESTRICTIVE path hona chahiye jo content/scheduledAt edit ke `POST_ALREADY_DISPATCHED` check se BYPASS kare.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate ek documented gap ko real feature design mein convert kar sakta hai, including non-obvious edge cases (add vs remove ki ALAG restrictiveness, fingerprint impact).
real_world_analogy: Ek guest list mein naya guest add karna (jo abhi tak invite hi nahi hua) hamesha fine hai, chahe baaki guests ko already invite bheji ja chuki ho. Par kisi EXISTING guest ko list se hatana (jisko already invite mil gayi hai) ek alag concern hai -- unhe explicitly 'disinvite' karna padega.
how_it_works: removeChannels reuses cancelChannel's pending-check logic per channel. addChannels validates new channels and creates fresh ChannelDelivery records (attempts: 0), bypassing the attempts>0 restriction that blocks content/scheduledAt edits, since a brand-new channel has nothing to 'un-see'.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka editPost (current content/scheduledAt-only shape), EditPostRequest interface, cancelChannel (reused logic for remove), schedulePost (reused validation for add).
advantages: Removes the need for the 'cancel the whole post and reschedule a new one' workaround, keeping one logical campaign under one post id
Add and remove reuse existing, already-tested validation logic (schedulePost's channel checks, cancelChannel's pending checks) rather than duplicating it
disadvantages: Adding a channel mid-flight changes the post's channel SET, which breaks the idempotency fingerprint's assumption that channels are fixed at creation -- the fingerprint would need to be recomputed or the feature kept entirely outside idempotency's scope
Significantly more edge cases than the current content/scheduledAt-only editPost (e.g. adding a channel that was previously removed)
common_mistakes: Blocking addChannels behind the same attempts>0 check that blocks content edits -- a brand-new channel has nothing to un-see and should not be blocked by a sibling's prior attempts
Forgetting that the new channel's nextAttemptAt must track the CURRENT scheduledAt, not some stale value, if scheduledAt is also being edited in the same call
follow_up_questions: Should re-adding a previously-removed (canceled) channel reuse its old ChannelDelivery record or create a fresh one?
How does this feature interact with the idempotency fingerprint, which currently bakes the channel set in at schedule time?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Treating add and remove as asymmetric operations (add bypasses the attempts-restriction, remove reuses cancel's stricter pending-only rule) matches the project's existing philosophy (SOC-104's cancel-vs-edit asymmetry) but adds a THIRD distinct rule to learn, alongside cancel's and edit's existing two.
advanced.failure_scenarios: If addChannels were allowed to re-target a channel that is currently mid-retry on another provider instance of the SAME channel key (not possible today since deliveries is keyed by channel name, but worth stating), the design must guarantee exactly one ChannelDelivery per channel key, never two.
advanced.alternatives: Keep the current 'cancel and reschedule a new post' workaround as a documented pattern instead of building this feature, if the complexity (especially the idempotency fingerprint interaction) outweighs the convenience for this project's actual use cases.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: This feature's complexity is per-post, not traffic-scale-dependent -- it does not get harder at 10x or 100x volume. What DOES get harder at scale is reasoning about the idempotency fingerprint once channel sets become mutable, since replay-matching logic (SOC-118) assumed the channel set never changes after schedule time.
advanced.production_improvements: If built, exclude addChannels/removeChannels from idempotency fingerprint comparisons entirely (treat edits as mutations outside the original fingerprint's scope, same as content/scheduledAt edits already are), and document clearly that a replay of the ORIGINAL schedulePost call still only matches the ORIGINAL channel set, not any edited one.

question: If this scheduler were deployed with multiple instances behind a load balancer (not even calling tick() concurrently, just handling schedulePost/cancelChannel calls), what breaks, and why is the dispatching Set the wrong thing to fix it with?
answer_hinglish:
Sabse fundamental problem: `SocialScheduler`'s SAARI state -- `posts`, `idempotency`, `dispatching` -- sab IN-MEMORY Maps/Sets HAIN, PER-INSTANCE. Agar do instances (A aur B) ek load balancer ke peeche hain, EK clientRequestId ke saath do requests A aur B par ALAG-ALAG land kar sakti hain -- A ko iska pata hi nahi hoga ki B ne already same clientRequestId process kar liya hai, kyunki A ka `idempotency` Map sirf A ki apni memory mein hai. Result: DUPLICATE posts, same clientRequestId ke saath, idempotency guarantee COMPLETELY BROKEN cross-instance.

`dispatching` Set yahan HELP NAHI karega, kyunki uska PURPOSE hi different hai -- woh sirf SAME-PROCESS overlap (ek slow provider + doosra tick() call, SAME instance ke andar) ke against protect karta hai. Yeh ek IN-MEMORY, PER-PROCESS synchronization primitive hai -- do ALAG processes ke beech koi visibility hi nahi hai ek doosre ke `dispatching` Set ki. Agar A aur B dono `tick()` chalayen apne-apne in-memory `posts` copies par (jo already divergent hain), har instance apna khud ka `dispatching` tracking karega, par woh DOOSRE instance ke concurrent dispatch ko kabhi dekh hi nahi payega.

Actual fix: `posts`/`idempotency`/`dispatching` teeno SHARED, EXTERNAL state mein jaane chahiye (database + distributed lock/lease mechanism, jaisa SOC-124 discuss karta hai project 21's JobQueue reuse ke saath). `dispatching` Set jaisa in-memory guard SIRF single-process ke liye sahi hai -- cross-process coordination ke liye ek GENUINELY shared mechanism chahiye (DB row lock, Redis lock, ya lease-based claim jaisa SOC-124/110).
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate samajhta hai ki ek IN-MEMORY, SINGLE-PROCESS guard (dispatching Set) GENUINELY distributed coordination ka substitute NAHI hai -- yeh common mistake hai jo engineers karte hain jab single-process code ko naively horizontally scale karte hain.
real_world_analogy: Do alag bank branches, jinke paas apna-apna SEPARATE ledger hai (koi shared database nahi), dono ek hi account number ke liye withdrawal process kar sakte hain SIMULTANEOUSLY -- har branch ko lagta hai woh pehla hai, kyunki dono ko doosre branch ki activity ka pata hi nahi hai. Ek branch ke andar ek 'teller is busy' sign (dispatching Set jaisa) doosre branch ko kabhi nahi dikhega.
how_it_works: posts/idempotency/dispatching are all per-process in-memory state today. Multiple instances mean multiple independent copies of this state with zero cross-instance visibility -- the dispatching Set's guarantee (same-process overlap protection) simply does not extend across a network boundary.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka SocialScheduler constructor -- the posts/idempotency/dispatching fields, all declared as in-process Map/Set with no external backing.
advantages: In-memory state is extremely fast and simple for a single-process deployment, which is this project's actual stage 1 scope
Identifying this limitation clearly (rather than papering over it with a same-process-only fix) avoids a false sense of safety
disadvantages: Zero horizontal scalability as built -- any multi-instance deployment silently breaks idempotency, dispatch-overlap protection, and basic data consistency (one instance's cancelChannel is invisible to another)
The failure mode (duplicate posts, double-dispatch) is SILENT -- there is no error or crash, just quietly wrong behavior
common_mistakes: Believing the dispatching Set or the idempotency Map provide any cross-process safety -- they are explicitly process-local
Scaling horizontally by just running more instances of this class without first moving its state to a shared backend
follow_up_questions: What is the minimal shared-state change needed to make just schedulePost's idempotency check safe across multiple instances, without touching tick()?
Why would a distributed lock (e.g. Redis) for the idempotency check alone not be enough to fix cross-instance dispatch overlap too?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Keeping all state in-process is the right call for THIS project's stated scope (a library, single caller, interview-focused) -- the mistake would be assuming this design 'mostly works' under multiple instances. Making it genuinely multi-instance-safe means replacing every one of posts/idempotency/dispatching with a shared, consistent backend, which is a different project, not a small patch.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Under a load balancer with 2+ instances: (1) duplicate posts from idempotency misses across instances, (2) a channel dispatched twice if two instances' tick() calls both see it as due and neither's dispatching Set knows about the other, (3) a cancelChannel call landing on instance B while the channel is mid-send on instance A succeeding silently (no DISPATCH_IN_PROGRESS, since B's dispatching Set is empty for that key) -- the exact race the guard exists to prevent, now bypassed entirely by the deployment topology.
advanced.alternatives: A shared database for posts/idempotency with transactional writes; a distributed lock (Redis, or a DB advisory lock) for mutual exclusion during dispatch; or routing all writes for a given postId to a single instance (sharding by postId) so no cross-instance coordination is needed at all for that post's operations.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: This is not really a '10x vs 100x' scaling question -- it breaks the MOMENT a second instance exists, regardless of traffic volume. The question that scales is how much contention a shared backend can handle once correctness is restored.
advanced.production_improvements: Before any multi-instance deployment: move posts/idempotency to a shared durable store with the right consistency guarantees (SOC-124's job-queue design for dispatch, a transactional store for schedulePost's idempotency check). Document clearly, as this question's analysis does, that today's SocialScheduler is single-process-only.

question: Write a function deadLetteredChannels(scheduler, postId): string[] using only the public API.
answer_hinglish:
Yeh exercise public API ko correctly navigate karna test karta hai -- `getPost` se poora post object milta hai (ya `undefined` agar postId exist nahi karta), aur `post.deliveries` ek `Record<string, ChannelDelivery>` hai jisko `Object.values()` se iterate karna hota hai har delivery ka `status` check karne ke liye.

Unknown postId ka handling important hai: `getPost` `undefined` return karta hai (throw nahi karta), isliye function ko bhi gracefully empty array return karna chahiye, exception nahi throw karni chahiye -- yeh is project ke 'read' methods (`getPost`, `list`) ka consistent behavior hai, sirf MUTATING methods (`cancelChannel`, `editPost`, etc.) UNKNOWN_POST throw karte hain.

Function khud ek simple filter+map hai: `Object.values(post.deliveries).filter(d => d.status === 'dead_letter').map(d => d.channel)`. Koi mutation nahi hoti, koi internal state access nahi -- poora public `ScheduledPost`/`ChannelDelivery` shape se kaam chal jaata hai, jo ScheduledPost already export karta hai index.ts se.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate public API shape (deliveries ek Record hai, Array nahi) sahi se handle kar sakta hai, including the undefined-vs-throw distinction between read and mutating methods.
real_world_analogy: Ek dashboard jo ek order ke saare shipped-but-returned items dhoondta hai -- order na mile toh empty list dikhata hai, crash nahi karta.
how_it_works: getPost(postId) returns ScheduledPost | undefined. Object.values(post.deliveries) gives every ChannelDelivery; filter by status === 'dead_letter', map to .channel.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka getPost method aur src/types.ts ka ScheduledPost.deliveries shape.
advantages: Uses only the public, documented API -- no access to private scheduler internals
Handles an unknown postId gracefully, matching getPost's own undefined-not-throw contract
disadvantages: Returns channel NAMES only, without the lastError reason -- a caller wanting diagnostics would need to re-derive that from the full deliveries object themselves
common_mistakes: Assuming deliveries is an array and calling .filter() directly on it, when it is actually a Record keyed by channel
Throwing on an unknown postId instead of returning an empty array, inconsistent with getPost's own contract
