How would you write this same function across EVERY post in the scheduler, not just one?

question: Write a function that computes the worst-case number of tick() calls a channel needs before it reaches a terminal state, given maxAttempts (assuming the caller advances the clock to exactly each next due time between calls).
answer_hinglish:
Key insight: HAR `tick()` call, jab clock exactly due time par advance kiya jaaye, EXACTLY EK attempt use karta hai ek channel ke liye -- chahe backoff kitna bhi bada ho, woh sirf YEH decide karta hai KAB next tick() due hoga, kitne tick() CALLS chahiye honge yeh nahi badalta. Isliye worst case (channel HAMESHA fail hota hai har attempt par) mein, exactly `maxAttempts` tick() calls chahiye honge dead_letter tak pahunchne ke liye -- pehla tick() attempt 1, doosra attempt 2, ... akhri tick() attempt maxAttempts (jahan `attempts >= maxAttempts` ho jaata hai aur dead_letter set hota hai).

Yeh `backoffMs` formula se INDEPENDENT hai -- `initialBackoffMs`/`maxBackoffMs` sirf TIME determine karte hain (kitna clock advance karna padega), COUNT nahi. Function khud trivial hai validation ke saath -- same validation jo `SocialScheduler`'s constructor already karta hai `maxAttempts >= 1` ke liye, consistency ke liye reuse kiya gaya hai.

Yeh function test karne ka tarika: ek scheduler banao `AlwaysFailsProvider` ke saath given `maxAttempts`, phir actual worst-case ticks GINO (har backoff ke baad clock advance karte hue) jab tak `dead_letter` na ho jaaye, aur compare karo function ke output se -- yeh exactly SOC-134 ka settle() helper pattern use karta hai.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate backoffMs aur maxAttempts ke beech ka RELATIONSHIP samajhta hai -- backoff sirf TIMING affect karta hai, tick() CALL COUNT nahi.
real_world_analogy: Ek exam mein tumhe max 5 attempts milte hain pass karne ke liye, chahe har attempt ke beech wait time 1 din ho ya 1 hafta -- wait time badalne se tumhare TOTAL ATTEMPTS ki ginti nahi badalti, sirf poora process kitne CALENDAR time lega yeh badalta hai.
how_it_works: Each tick() call, assuming the caller advances the clock to exactly the next due time, consumes exactly one attempt for a channel that keeps failing. So the worst case is simply maxAttempts tick() calls, independent of backoff values.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka dispatchChannel (one attempt per dispatch) aur tick() (one dispatch per due channel per call); test/tick.test.ts ka 'exhausting maxAttempts' test demonstrates this count directly.
advantages: Trivial, O(1) computation once you see that backoff timing and attempt count are independent concerns
Directly useful for capacity planning (SOC-114): tells you the upper bound on tick() calls a single stubbornly-failing channel will ever consume
disadvantages: Assumes the caller always advances the clock to exactly the next due time -- in a real deployment with periodic polling, the ACTUAL number of tick() calls could be higher if polling is less frequent than the backoff interval
common_mistakes: Trying to compute this from the backoff formula (summing delays) instead of realizing the answer is simply maxAttempts
Forgetting the constructor-level validation (maxAttempts must be an integer >= 1), producing a nonsensical result for invalid input
follow_up_questions: How would this answer change if tick() were called on a FIXED interval (e.g. every 30 seconds) instead of exactly at each due time?
How would you write a test using ManualClock that proves this worst-case number against a real AlwaysFailsProvider?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: This question's answer only holds under the idealized assumption of 'clock advanced to exactly the next due time' -- a real production polling interval decouples CLOCK time from CALL count, so this exercise is a theoretical bound, not an operational guarantee.
advanced.failure_scenarios: If a real deployment polls tick() less frequently than the computed backoff delay, a channel could sit well past its nextAttemptAt without being dispatched sooner -- the channel still only consumes maxAttempts total dispatches, but the WALL-CLOCK time to reach dead_letter grows with the polling gap.
advanced.alternatives: A more operationally useful metric would be worst-case WALL-CLOCK time to dead_letter (summing backoffMs across all attempts, capped), rather than tick() call count, since that is what actually matters for monitoring/alerting SLAs.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: This bound is per-channel and traffic-independent -- it does not change at 10x or 100x post volume. What changes at scale is how many channels are SIMULTANEOUSLY in this worst case at once, which is a tick() throughput concern (SOC-114), not a per-channel count concern.
advanced.production_improvements: Pair this theoretical bound with a real wall-clock-time calculation (sum of backoffMs across attempts, capped at maxBackoffMs each) to give on-call engineers a concrete 'this channel will be stuck retrying for at most X minutes' answer.

question: Write a test proving that canceling a channel mid-retry stops all future dispatch attempts for it.
answer_hinglish:
Yeh test SOC-104's trade-off ko DIRECTLY exercise karta hai -- cancel ek 'still pending' channel par kaam karta hai CHAHE woh mid-retry ho (attempts > 0). Test ka structure: PEHLE ek channel ko fail karo EK baar (attempts=1, status pending, retry ka wait), phir usse CANCEL karo, phir clock ko BAHUT aage advance karo (far past any backoff), phir tick() call karo -- aur ASSERT karo ki provider ko DOBARA call hi nahi kiya gaya.

Key assertion do parts mein hai: (1) `mastodon.attempts` (provider ka internal call log) ki LENGTH same rehti hai cancel se PEHLE aur BAAD mein -- yeh PROVES ki koi naya `send()` call nahi hua. (2) `scheduler.getPost(...)` ka status `canceled` reh jaata hai, `pending` ya kuch aur nahi ban jaata.

Yeh pattern EXACTLY `test/tick.test.ts`'s 'exhausting maxAttempts' test se milta hai (jo bhi provider call count ko before/after compare karta hai), par yahan termination CANCEL se hoti hai, maxAttempts exhaustion se nahi -- isliye attempts count SIRF 1 par RUK jaata hai, 3 ya 5 tak nahi badhta.
why_needed: Interviewer ek REAL test likhwana chahta hai jo mid-retry cancel ka exact guarantee prove kare, provider call count assertion ke through -- sirf status check se yeh PROOF nahi milta ki provider dobara call NAHI hua.
real_world_analogy: Ek factory worker jisko ek order ke liye retry karte waqt BEECH mein rok diya jaaye -- test karne ka sahi tarika yeh hai ki worker ka ACTUAL output (parts banaye) count karo, sirf uska status board check karna kaafi nahi, kyunki status board galat bhi ho sakta hai.
how_it_works: Schedule a post with an always-failing provider -> tick() once (attempts=1, still pending) -> cancelChannel() mid-retry -> advance the clock far past any backoff -> tick() again -> assert the provider's call count is unchanged and status stays canceled.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka cancelChannel aur tick(); test/cancel-edit.test.ts ka existing cancelChannel describe block (same pattern, different assertion focus); src/providers.ts ka AlwaysFailsProvider.attempts array.
advantages: Asserts on the PROVIDER's call log, not just the delivery status -- proves the provider was genuinely never called again, not just that the status label looks right
Advancing the clock far beyond any backoff window rules out 'it just hasn't become due again yet' as an alternative explanation
disadvantages: Does not cover the DISPATCH_IN_PROGRESS race (cancel while a send is actually mid-flight) -- that is test/dispatch-guard.test.ts's job, a separate concern
common_mistakes: Only checking the delivery's status after cancel, without also advancing the clock and ticking again to prove no further dispatch happens
Canceling the channel BEFORE any attempt (attempts=0), which would not actually exercise the 'mid-retry' scenario at all
follow_up_questions: How would you adapt this test to use cancelPost instead of cancelChannel?
What would need to change in this test to also prove the SIBLING channel of a multi-channel post is unaffected by this cancel?

question: Write a function pendingChannelCount(scheduler): number that counts every pending channel across every post.
answer_hinglish:
Yeh exercise do levels ki iteration test karta hai -- `scheduler.list()` saare posts ka ARRAY deta hai (`ScheduledPost[]`), aur har post ke `deliveries` ek Record hai jisko phir se `Object.values()` se iterate karna hota hai. Yeh EXACTLY `tick()`'s apna internal scan jaisa double-loop hai (SOC-115 dekho), bas yahan filter 'pending AND due' ke bajaye sirf 'pending' hai (koi `nextAttemptAt` check nahi, koi `dispatching` check nahi).

Function khud ek simple accumulator hai: har post ke har delivery ko check karo, `status === 'pending'` ho toh counter badhao. Koi mutation nahi, `list()` already `structuredClone` se safe copies deta hai (`toPublicPost` internally use karta hai), isliye yeh function scheduler ki internal state ko kabhi touch nahi karta.

Yeh BACKLOG metric ka EK building block hai (SOC-113 mein poora backlog-with-staleness discuss hua), par yahan sirf RAW COUNT hai, 'due' filter ke bina -- matlab ek post jo abhi 5 minute baad due hai, woh BHI count hota hai (kyunki woh 'pending' hai), chahe woh ABHI dispatch-ready na ho.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate list() ka public shape (array of posts, each with a deliveries Record) sahi se navigate kar sakta hai, aur 'pending' ko 'due' se distinguish kar sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek poore mall ke har store mein kitne customers abhi queue mein khade hain, unhe COUNT karna -- chahe unka turn abhi aaya ho ya nahi, 'queue mein hona' matter karta hai, 'turn aa gaya' nahi.
how_it_works: scheduler.list() returns every ScheduledPost. For each, Object.values(post.deliveries) gives every ChannelDelivery; count those with status === 'pending', summed across all posts.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka list() method; src/types.ts ka ScheduledPost.deliveries shape.
advantages: Simple, readable double-loop, matching tick()'s own scan structure closely enough to be instantly recognizable
Works entirely off the public list()/deliveries shape, no private state access needed
disadvantages: Does not distinguish 'pending and due' from 'pending but not yet due' -- for that, SOC-113's richer backlog function is needed instead
O(total deliveries across all posts) every call, same complexity concern as tick()'s own scan (SOC-114)
common_mistakes: Counting posts instead of individual channel deliveries (a post with 3 pending channels should add 3, not 1)
Confusing this with a due-only backlog count -- this counts ALL pending, including ones not yet due
follow_up_questions: How would you modify this to only count channels that are both pending AND due right now?
How would you make this O(1) if it needed to be queried very frequently, instead of scanning everything each call?

question: Write a settle() helper that advances a ManualClock and calls tick() repeatedly until every channel of every post reaches a terminal state, with a round budget to avoid an infinite loop.
answer_hinglish:
Yeh exercise `test/invariants.test.ts`'s ACTUAL `settle()` helper ka pattern follow karta hai -- yeh ek realistic 'simulate the whole system to completion' utility hai jo randomized tests mein use hota hai. Logic: HAR round mein, saare posts scan karo, dhoondo SABSE CHHOTA `nextAttemptAt` jo abhi bhi PENDING hai (`anyPending` flag se track karo ki kuch pending bacha hai ya nahi). Agar kuch pending nahi bacha, RETURN (already settled). Agar bacha hai, clock ko us NEXT DUE TIME tak advance karo (`clock.advance(nextDue - clock.now())`, SIRF agar woh future mein hai), phir `tick()` call karo.

`maxAttempts` FINITE hai, isliye HAR channel jo canceled nahi hua, EVENTUALLY terminal (sent ya dead_letter) ho jaayega -- isliye yeh loop BOUNDED hai theoretically, par ek `maxRounds` safety limit zaroori hai taaki ek GENUINE BUG (jaise ek channel jo kabhi terminal na ho) infinite loop na bana de test suite ko hang karne ke liye.

Yeh helper standalone bhi useful hai (SOC-130 jaisa exercise isko use kar sakta hai verify karne ke liye), aur yeh dikhata hai ki is project ka POLLED `tick()` model (koi internal timer) kaise manually driven jaata hai tests mein -- koi real `setTimeout`/sleep kabhi nahi lagta.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate 'advance to fixed point' pattern design kar sakta hai -- yeh is project ki pura test-design philosophy ka core hai (ManualClock + polled tick()).
real_world_analogy: Ek simulation jo ek vending machine ke poore din ka operation FAST-FORWARD karti hai -- sirf AGLE important moment (jab koi coin daalega, jab koi item restock hoga) tak time jump karti hai, bina har second ko individually simulate kiye.
how_it_works: Each round: scan all posts for the minimum nextAttemptAt among still-pending deliveries. If none are pending, return (settled). Otherwise advance the clock to that minimum (if it's in the future) and call tick(). Repeat up to maxRounds.
in_this_project: test/invariants.test.ts ka existing settle() function -- this exercise reproduces its exact pattern; src/clock.ts ka ManualClock.advance().
advantages: Deterministically drives the whole system to completion without any real sleeps, keeping tests fast
The maxRounds safety net turns a potential infinite loop (from a real bug) into a clear, fast-failing test instead of a hang
disadvantages: Assumes every pending channel will eventually terminate within maxRounds -- a pathological maxAttempts/backoff combination could need tuning of that bound
Advances the clock to the EARLIEST due time across ALL posts each round, which can mean many rounds if posts have very staggered due times
common_mistakes: Forgetting the `if (nextDue > clock.now())` guard, which could try to advance the clock backwards or by zero unnecessarily
Not having a maxRounds bound at all, risking a genuine infinite loop if some future bug introduces a channel that never reaches a terminal state
follow_up_questions: Why is this pattern necessary for invariants.test.ts's randomized test specifically, versus the simpler hand-advanced clock steps used in tick.test.ts?
What would happen to this helper if a canceled channel were somehow left with status 'pending' by a bug -- would settle() hang or fail fast?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: A generic settle() helper trades a little bit of per-test flexibility (you cannot easily inspect intermediate states between rounds without instrumenting it) for a huge reduction in test duplication across randomized and exploratory tests -- this project's invariants.test.ts relies on exactly this trade.
advanced.failure_scenarios: If a real bug introduced a channel that stays 'pending' forever (e.g. a dead-letter condition that never fires due to an off-by-one), settle() would exhaust maxRounds and throw a clear, fast error -- much better than a silent infinite loop or a flaky timeout failure.
advanced.alternatives: A per-post settle (only advancing/ticking until ONE specific post is done) instead of a global one, useful when a test only cares about one post among many unrelated ones in the same scheduler.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At 10x-100x posts, this helper's per-round scan cost grows the same way tick()'s own scan does (SOC-114) -- for very large randomized tests, the number of distinct nextAttemptAt values (and thus rounds) could also grow, making maxRounds tuning more important.
advanced.production_improvements: None needed in production -- this is purely a test utility. If reused across many test files, it is worth extracting into a shared test-helpers module (this project's test/queued-helpers.ts in project 21 is a precedent for that pattern).

question: Write a function postsWithDeadLetters(scheduler) that returns, for every post with at least one dead-lettered channel, its postId and the list of dead-lettered channel names.
answer_hinglish:
Yeh exercise SOC-129's single-post version ka MULTI-POST extension hai -- har post ke liye `deadLetteredChannels`-jaisa filter apply karo, par is baar sirf un posts ko RESULT mein include karo jinke paas KAM SE KAM EK dead-lettered channel hai (empty-result posts ko skip karo, poori list clutter na ho).

Logic: `scheduler.list()` se saare posts lo, har post ke `deliveries` ko filter karo `status === 'dead_letter'` ke liye, map karo `.channel` nikalne ke liye. Agar resulting array `length > 0` hai, result mein `{ postId: post.id, channels }` push karo -- agar `length === 0`, us post ko SKIP karo (yeh healthy post hai, report mein noise nahi daalna).

Yeh function EXACTLY ek PRODUCTION monitoring tool jaisa use case hai (SOC-111 ka dead-letter-rate-per-channel ka precursor) -- 'kaunse posts abhi incomplete hain kyunki unka ek channel permanently fail ho gaya' turant dikha deta hai, ek on-call engineer ke liye SOC-112's checklist ka ek concrete tool.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate ek single-post utility ko MULTI-post aggregation mein extend kar sakta hai, aur 'only include non-empty results' filtering logic correctly apply kar sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek warehouse manager ka report jo SIRF un orders ko list karta hai jinka KAM SE KAM EK item permanently out-of-stock hai -- poori tarah fulfilled orders ya abhi-processing orders is report mein nahi dikhte, sirf genuinely problematic ones.
how_it_works: For each post from scheduler.list(), filter its deliveries for status === 'dead_letter' and map to channel names. Only include the post in the result if that filtered list is non-empty.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka list() method; src/types.ts ka ChannelDelivery.status.
advantages: Only surfaces genuinely problematic posts, keeping the result focused and useful for a human or alerting system to act on
Reuses the same filter pattern as SOC-129's single-post version, just wrapped in an outer loop -- easy to recognize and maintain
disadvantages: Does not include lastError reasons -- a caller wanting root-cause context has to go back to post.deliveries themselves
O(total deliveries) scan, same as every other list()-based utility in this project (SOC-114's concern applies here too at large scale)
common_mistakes: Including EVERY post in the result with an empty channels array instead of skipping posts with no dead letters
Returning the full ChannelDelivery objects instead of just the channel name strings, when the question specifically asks for channel names
follow_up_questions: How would you extend this to also include each dead-lettered channel's lastError for root-cause triage?
How would you turn this into a periodic monitoring job that alerts when the result's length grows past a threshold?

question: Write a function sentChannelsForPost(scheduler, postId): { channel: string; providerId: string; sentAt: number }[] that returns the delivery details of every successfully sent channel for one post.
answer_hinglish:
Yeh exercise TYPE NARROWING ka ek acha example hai -- `ChannelDelivery` ke `providerId`/`sentAt` fields OPTIONAL hain type definition mein (`providerId?: string; sentAt?: number`) kyunki woh sirf `status === 'sent'` hone PAR set hote hain. Isliye function ko sirf `status === 'sent'` filter karna hi KAAFI nahi -- TypeScript ko bhi explicitly batana padta hai (ya runtime assertion) ki in deliveries ke paas yeh fields DEFINITELY set hain.

Safe approach: filter karo `status === 'sent'`, phir map karte waqt `providerId!`/`sentAt!` use karo (non-null assertion) -- yeh SAFE hai kyunki `dispatchChannel`'s code GUARANTEE karta hai ki `status = 'sent'` set hone se PEHLE `providerId`/`sentAt` dono already assign ho chuke hote hain (same statement block mein, sequentially).

Unknown postId ka handling SOC-129 jaisa hi hai -- `getPost` undefined return karta hai, function empty array return kare, throw na kare.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate optional fields ko SAFELY narrow kar sakta hai jab unka presence ek STATUS value se guaranteed ho, aur is guarantee ko actual source code se justify kar sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek parcel ka tracking number sirf TAB available hota hai jab parcel 'shipped' status mein pahunch jaaye -- agar status 'shipped' hai, tumhe PATA hai tracking number zaroor hoga, isliye usse safely access kar sakte ho bina null check kiye.
how_it_works: getPost(postId) -> if undefined, return []. Otherwise filter Object.values(deliveries) for status === 'sent', then map each to { channel, providerId: d.providerId!, sentAt: d.sentAt! }, relying on dispatchChannel's guarantee that both fields are set before status becomes 'sent'.
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts ka getPost aur dispatchChannel (where providerId/sentAt are set together with status='sent'); src/types.ts ka ChannelDelivery's optional providerId/sentAt fields.
advantages: Correctly relies on the status==='sent' invariant to safely narrow optional fields, instead of adding unnecessary runtime null checks
Returns a clean, purpose-shaped result rather than the full ChannelDelivery with every other status-specific field
disadvantages: The non-null assertions (!) trust dispatchChannel's invariant rather than verifying it at runtime -- if that invariant were ever violated by a future bug, this function would produce a runtime error instead of a type error
common_mistakes: Using optional chaining (d.providerId ?? 'unknown') instead of asserting, which silently hides a genuine bug if the invariant is ever broken
Forgetting the status filter entirely and trying to map providerId/sentAt off every delivery, most of which won't have them set
follow_up_questions: Why is it safe here to use the non-null assertion operator instead of an explicit runtime check?
How would you write a mutation-style test proving dispatchChannel always sets providerId and sentAt together with status='sent', never one without the other?

question: Why does dispatchChannel check `result.retryable === false` rather than `!result.retryable` or `result.retryable !== true`?
answer_hinglish:
Kyunki field OPTIONAL hai aur rule hai 'absent matlab retryable'. Teen values possible hain: `undefined` (stage 1 providers, aur provider-throws wala catch path), `true`, aur `false`. Sirf `false` permanent hona chahiye.

`!result.retryable` aur `result.retryable !== true` dono `undefined` ko permanent bana dete. Matlab har stage-1 failure -- AlwaysFailsProvider ka default, FlakyProvider, ek throw -- attempt 1 par hi dead-letter ho jaati. FlakyProvider(2) wala channel jo 3rd attempt par succeed hona chahiye tha, kabhi retry hi nahi hota. Yeh exactly woh backward-compat break hai jisse bachne ke liye field optional rakha gaya tha.

`=== false` strict equality hai, koi coercion nahi -- sirf literal boolean false match karta hai. Mutation pass mein isi line ke variations try kiye gaye: R1 (`!== false`, inverted) aur R4 (`retryable == null`, jo undefined/missing ko permanent maanta hai) -- dono caught, kyunki stage 1 ke retry tests (exhausts maxAttempts, flaky sibling) turant fail ho jaate hain.

General lesson: ek optional boolean jiska default `true` hai, uske liye explicit `=== false` likho; jiska default `false` hai, uske liye `=== true`. Truthiness check sirf tab safe hai jab 'absent' ka meaning bhi falsy wala ho.
why_needed: Optional fields ke saath truthiness bugs bahut common hain; interviewer dekhta hai ki tum undefined ko ek alag teesri state ki tarah treat karte ho ya nahi.
real_world_analogy: Ek form mein 'mujhe call mat karo' checkbox hai. Agar kisi ne checkbox chhua hi nahi (blank), tum use 'call mat karo' nahi maan sakte -- sirf tab jab usne explicitly tick kiya ho.
how_it_works: result.retryable undefined -> permanent false -> retry path (agar attempts < maxAttempts). true -> permanent false. false -> permanent true -> dead_letter usi attempt par. Catch path ka result `{ status: "failed", reason: "provider threw: ..." }` hai, retryable key ke bina -> retryable.

PLAN.md Stage 2: 'dispatchChannel checks result.retryable === false, not !== true'. README.md ka stage 2 mutation table: R1, R4.

Strict equality, no coercion surprises
Directly pinned by mutations R1 and R4
disadvantages: Reads less naturally than a truthiness check, so a future refactor might 'simplify' it -- only the comment and the mutation-backed tests guard it

Forgetting that the provider-throws catch path also produces a result with no retryable key

question: Why does a permanent failure still increment attempts, instead of being treated as 'not a real attempt'?
answer_hinglish:
Kyunki attempt SACH mein hua tha. `attempts` ka meaning hai 'provider.send() kitni baar actually call hua' -- types.ts ka comment literally yahi kehta hai -- na ki 'retry budget mein se kitna use hua'. Permanent failure mein bhi provider call hua aur usne jawab diya, toh counter badhna hi chahiye.

Doosri wajah mechanical hai: `attempts += 1` dispatchChannel mein await se PEHLE synchronously hota hai, jab abhi pata hi nahi ki result kya aayega. Yahi increment editPost ko 'already tried / in-flight' detect karne deta hai (attempts > 0 -> POST_ALREADY_DISPATCHED). Permanent failure ke baad decrement karna is signal ko ulta kar deta: jis channel ka provider content dekh chuka hai, woh attempts 0 dikhata aur editPost galti se allow ho jaata.

Teesri: ek counter, ek meaning. Decrement karte toh diagnostics, invariant test aur kisi future API ko 'real attempts' vs 'counted attempts' ke liye do fields chahiye hote. PLAN.md ke Stage 2 decisions mein yeh option explicitly reject kiya gaya.

Yeh mutation R13 se pinned hai ('attempts decremented back by one for a permanent failure') -- caught, kyunki permanent tests `attempts` ko 1 (aur mixed sequence mein 2) assert karte hain. Side benefit: dead_letter par `attempts < maxAttempts` khud ek hint hai ki give-up permanent failure se hua.
why_needed: Counters ka meaning precise rakhna ek senior signal hai; interviewer dekhta hai ki tum 'budget' aur 'history' ko mix karte ho ya nahi, aur increment ki timing ka race-detection se rishta samajhte ho.
real_world_analogy: Ek doctor ke clinic ne patient ko call kiya, patient ne bola 'main yeh number chhod chuka hoon'. Call log mein woh call dikhegi -- 'usne mana kar diya' ka matlab yeh nahi ki call hui hi nahi.
how_it_works: dispatchChannel: try { attempts += 1; result = await send({ ..., attempt: attempts }) } -> failed branch: lastError = reason; permanent check -> dead_letter. attempts kahin bhi ghatta nahi. First-attempt permanent failure ke baad ChannelDelivery.attempts === 1.
in_this_project: src/types.ts ChannelDelivery: `attempts: number; // how many times a provider.send() was actually called for this channel`. test/tick.test.ts 'dead-letters on the very first attempt, skipping the retry schedule entirely' `attempts` ko toBe(1) assert karta hai ('not 5'); 'attempt 1 retryable, attempt 2 permanent' toBe(2). README.md mutation R13.
advantages: attempts has one meaning everywhere it is read
editPost's already-tried / in-flight signal stays correct
attempts < maxAttempts on a dead_letter is itself a hint of an early (permanent) give-up
disadvantages: You cannot read 'retry budget used' separately from 'calls made' -- by design they are the same number
A permanent failure on the very last allowed attempt looks identical to exhausted retries
common_mistakes: Decrementing attempts for a permanent failure so it 'does not count' (mutation R13)
Moving the increment after the await, which breaks editPost's race detection
Treating attempts as a retry counter rather than a call counter
follow_up_questions: How can an operator tell a permanent dead-letter from an exhausted one using only attempts and maxAttempts?
When is that inference ambiguous?
Why must the increment happen before the await rather than after?

question: Symptom: after adding a permanently-failing provider to the randomized invariant test, its dead_letter check started failing. Why did the old rule break, how was it changed, and what does the new check still prove?
answer_hinglish:
Stage 1 ka invariant tha: har dead_letter delivery ke paas lastError hai aur `attempts === maxAttempts` -- kyunki tab dead-letter tak pahunchne ka EKLAUTA raasta saare attempts exhaust karna tha. Stage 2 ne mix mein ek chautha provider add kiya, `delta = new AlwaysFailsProvider(PERMANENT_REASON, false)`. Delta ka channel pehli attempt par dead-letter hota hai, attempts 1, jabki maxAttempts 3 hai -- purana assertion turant fail hota. Bug code mein nahi tha; invariant khud stage 1 ki ek assumption encode kar raha tha jo ab sach nahi thi.

Fix: checkPost ab dead_letter ko `lastError` ke basis par do cases mein todta hai. Agar `d.lastError === PERMANENT_REASON` (delta), toh attempts 1 aur maxAttempts ke beech hona chahiye; warna (gamma, default retryable always-fails) abhi bhi strict `attempts === maxAttempts`. Matlab retryable channels ke liye stage 1 ki poori guarantee intact hai -- agar permanent logic galti se ordinary failures ko bhi early dead-letter karne lage (jaise R3 ya R4), gamma ka check fail ho jaayega.

Ek honest observation: delta ka check ek range hai (`>= 1`, `<= maxAttempts`), jabki delta har attempt par permanently fail karta hai, toh uske attempts hamesha exactly 1 hone chahiye -- yeh assertion `toBe(1)` tak tight ki ja sakti hai. Abhi permanent-on-attempt-1 ka exact proof tick.test.ts ke dedicated tests dete hain.

Lesson: jab ek naya terminal path add ho, har woh invariant dobara padho jo 'X tak pahunchne ka sirf ek raasta hai' assume karta hai.
why_needed: Yeh dikhata hai ki tum ek failing test ko 'code bug' vs 'stale invariant' mein classify kar sakte ho -- aur invariant ko loosen karte waqt yeh ensure karte ho ki purani guarantee weak na ho.
real_world_analogy: Ek bank ka audit rule tha 'har closed account ka balance zero hai'. Phir 'fraud ki wajah se frozen-and-closed' ka naya raasta aaya jahan balance zero nahi hota. Rule ko hatana galat hai -- sahi yeh hai ki rule ko 'normal closure' aur 'fraud closure' mein split karo, aur normal waala utna hi strict rakho.
how_it_works: Har seed par 250 random operations (schedulePost / cancelChannel / cancelPost / clock advance + tick), phir settle() clock ko next due tak advance karke tick() karta hai jab tak koi pending na bache. Phir checkPost har delivery check karta hai: sent -> providerId + sentAt; dead_letter -> lastError truthy, aur PERMANENT_REASON ho toh 1..maxAttempts, warna === maxAttempts; canceled -> canceledAt.
in_this_project: test/invariants.test.ts: `const CHANNELS = ["alpha", "beta", "gamma", "delta"]` (always-succeeds, flaky(2), always-fails retryable, always-fails permanent), `PERMANENT_REASON = "delta: account permanently disconnected"`, maxAttempts 3, seeds 1-5, aur checkPost ka dead_letter branch. R3/R4 jaise breaks (har failure permanent, ya undefined bhi permanent) is branch ke gamma half ko bhi fail kar dete, kyunki gamma tab attempt 1 par dead-letter hota.
advantages: Retryable channels keep stage 1's strict exhausted-every-attempt guarantee
Permanent channels are exercised alongside cancels and flaky siblings across 5 seeds
Keying on a unique lastError makes the branch exact without peeking into provider internals
disadvantages: The permanent branch is a range, looser than the provider's real behaviour (always exactly 1)
Branching on a reason string couples the test to the fake provider's message
common_mistakes: Deleting the attempts assertion entirely to make the test green, losing the stage 1 guarantee
Loosening every dead_letter to `<= maxAttempts`, which would let R3/R4-style bugs slip through the invariant test
Assuming a failing invariant always means the production code is wrong
follow_up_questions: How would you tighten the delta branch, and what would that catch that the range does not?
Why key on lastError rather than on the channel name?
Which mutation would only the gamma half of this check catch?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Invariant ko split karna (permanent vs retryable) har path ki apni guarantee rakhta hai; ek single loose rule simple hota par stage 1 ka strongest check kho deta. Trade: test ab fake provider ke reason string par depend karta hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar koi future change permanent failures ko attempt 2 tak retry karne lage (off-by-one), range wala delta check pass ho jaayega -- sirf tick.test.ts ka 'dead-letters on the very first attempt' test pakdega. Isliye tighter toBe(1) defense-in-depth deta.
advanced.alternatives: ChannelDelivery par ek deadLetterCause field (tab test reason string ki jagah us field par branch karta, par woh production field abhi exist nahi karta); ya delta ke liye alag deterministic test aur random mix mein se usse hata dena (coverage ghatti).
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Zyada seeds/operations se combinations badhte hain par rule wahi rehta hai. Bade real system mein invariants ko per-cause metrics (permanent vs exhausted dead-letter counts) ke roop mein production mein bhi monitor karna useful hota hai.
advanced.production_improvements: Delta branch ko `toBe(1)` tak tight karna, aur agar deadLetterCause field add ho toh invariant ko usse cross-check karna (cause 'permanent' => attempts <= maxAttempts, 'exhausted' => attempts === maxAttempts).

question: Why is the permanently-failing fake a constructor option on AlwaysFailsProvider instead of a new provider class, and why does it only emit the retryable key when it is false?
answer_hinglish:
Class vs option ka line is file mein stage 1 se hi khincha hua hai: FlakyProvider ka `failCount` ek constructor option hai, koi `FailsTwiceThenSucceedsProvider` / `FailsOnceThenSucceedsProvider` family nahi. Rule: naya class tab jab naya BEHAVIOR ho; same behavior ka configuration ho toh constructor knob. 'Always fails' already woh ek behavior hai jo AlwaysFailsProvider model karta hai -- failure retryable hai ya permanent, yeh usi behavior ki configuration hai. Isliye signature bana `constructor(reason = "...", retryable = true)`, aur ek `AlwaysFailsPermanentlyProvider` class reject hui (PLAN.md Stage 2 decisions).

Default `true` hone se har stage-1 call site -- `new AlwaysFailsProvider()` ya `new AlwaysFailsProvider("some reason")` -- bilkul same rehta hai.

Key sirf false par kyun? Kyunki types.ts ka contract hai 'omitting the field IS retryable'. Agar provider hamesha `retryable: true` explicitly bhejta, behavior same rehta par result ka SHAPE badal jaata -- aur providers.test.ts ka purana assertion `toEqual({ status: "failed", reason: "nope" })` fail ho jaata, kyunki toEqual extra defined key ko mismatch maanta hai. Sirf false par emit karne se stage 1 ka exact shape preserve hota hai, aur naya test 'defaults to retryable: true, and does not put a retryable field on the result at all' isko pin karta hai. Mutations R9-R12 (default flip, ternary swap, condition negate, false ki jagah true) sab caught.

FlakyProvider untouched hai: woh ek temporarily-down platform model karta hai jo recover hota hai -- inherently retryable, toh usse permanent bolne ki koi wajah nahi.
why_needed: Test fakes ka design bhi API design hai; interviewer dekhta hai ki tum class explosion se bachte ho aur backward-compatible output shape ka dhyan rakhte ho.
real_world_analogy: Ek coffee machine mein 'sugar' ka knob hota hai, 'sugar wali machine' aur 'bina sugar wali machine' do alag machines nahi khareedte. Aur agar knob default par hai, machine receipt par 'sugar: normal' likhna shuru na kare -- purane receipt parsers confuse ho jaayenge.
how_it_works: AlwaysFailsProvider.send(): attempts mein message push, phir `this.retryable ? { status: "failed", reason } : { status: "failed", reason, retryable: false }`. dispatchChannel `=== false` check karta hai, toh absent aur true dono retryable treat hote hain.
in_this_project: src/providers.ts::AlwaysFailsProvider ka constructor aur send(), uske upar ka comment ('a constructor option rather than a separate provider class because always fails is already the one behavior this class models'). test/providers.test.ts ke do naye tests. src/demo.ts: `new AlwaysFailsProvider("account disconnected", false)` instagram channel ke liye. README.md mutations R9-R12.
advantages: No class explosion; matches the existing FlakyProvider failCount precedent
Every stage 1 call site and shape assertion is untouched
The permanent variant is one argument away in tests and the demo
disadvantages: A positional boolean (`new AlwaysFailsProvider("x", false)`) is less self-documenting at the call site than a named option or a class name
common_mistakes: Always emitting `retryable: true`, which changes the result shape and breaks the existing toEqual test
Adding a permanent mode to FlakyProvider too, even though a recovering platform is inherently retryable
Creating a new class per failure flavour
follow_up_questions: Would an options object `{ retryable: false }` be better than a positional boolean here?
Why would toEqual fail on an extra `retryable: true` key?
When WOULD a new provider class be the right call?

question: Write a function classifyDeadLetters(scheduler) that splits every dead-lettered channel into 'gave up early' (attempts < maxAttempts) and 'exhausted retries', using only the public API. When is the split ambiguous?
answer_hinglish:
Logic simple hai: `scheduler.list()` se saare posts lo, har post ke `deliveries` (ek Record, Array nahi -- isliye `Object.values`) par loop karo, sirf `status === "dead_letter"` wale lo. Agar `attempts < maxAttempts`, woh 'early' bucket mein -- kyunki stage 2 ke baad early give-up ka sirf ek hi raasta hai: provider ne `retryable: false` bola. Warna 'exhausted' bucket. Har row mein postId, channel, attempts aur lastError rakho taaki on-call engineer turant reason dekh sake (jaise 'account disconnected').

Ambiguity: agar permanent failure EXACTLY last allowed attempt par aaye (jaise attempt 1 aur 2 retryable fail, attempt 3 par retryable: false, maxAttempts 3), toh attempts === maxAttempts hoga aur yeh 'exhausted' mein classify hoga -- jabki actual cause permanent tha. Public API par koi field nahi hai jo yeh fark bataye; ChannelDelivery mein dead-letter ka cause store hi nahi hota. Isliye 'early' bucket hamesha permanent hai, par 'exhausted' bucket mein bhi kuch permanent ho sakte hain. Is gap ko band karne ke liye production mein ek deadLetterCause field chahiye (is project mein nahi hai).

Yeh exercise SOC-129/SOC-134 ke dead-letter helpers ka extension hai, par ab stage 2 ke do dead-letter paths ko alag karta hai -- operationally bahut useful, kyunki 'early' wale ko retry karne se koi fayda nahi (credentials fix karo), jabki 'exhausted' wale shayad provider recover hone par naye post se resend kiye ja sakte hain.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhta hai ki tum public API se derived data nikaal sakte ho aur uski limits honestly bata sakte ho -- yahan exactly woh case jahan available fields cause ko uniquely identify nahi karte.
real_world_analogy: Courier ke returned packages: jo pehli ya doosri try mein hi 'address exist nahi karta' bol kar laut aaye, woh clearly address problem hain. Jo teeno try ke baad laute, unme zyaadatar 'ghar par koi nahi tha' hain -- par kuch aise bhi ho sakte hain jahan teesri try par pata chala ki address hi galat hai.
how_it_works: O(total deliveries) scan, koi mutation nahi, sirf read methods (list) use hote hain. Classification rule: dead_letter && attempts < maxAttempts => early (permanent by construction); dead_letter && attempts === maxAttempts => exhausted (ya last-attempt permanent).
in_this_project: src/scheduler.ts::list public read API hai; src/types.ts::ChannelDelivery ke fields attempts, maxAttempts, lastError, status. Early dead-letter sirf dispatchChannel ke `permanent ||` clause se possible hai. test/tick.test.ts ka 'attempt 1 retryable, attempt 2 permanent' case maxAttempts 5 ke saath attempts 2 deta hai -> 'early'.

The 'early' bucket is exact: it can only contain permanent failures
Gives on-call an actionable split (fix credentials vs maybe resend later)
disadvantages: The 'exhausted' bucket can hide a permanent failure that happened on the last allowed attempt
Full scan over every post on each call; fine in memory, not for a large persisted store
common_mistakes: Iterating post.deliveries as if it were an array
Claiming the 'exhausted' bucket is purely retryable failures
Classifying by parsing lastError strings instead of attempts vs maxAttempts
